title: Setting, Structure & Narrative
content_html:
London as a Gothic Landscape

Stevenson transforms London into a character in its own right. The city in Jekyll and Hyde is fog-choked, gas-lit, and full of shadows. The most famous description captures this perfectly: “The fog still slept on the wing above the drowned city.” The personification of fog as a sleeping creature hovering over a “drowned” city creates an oppressive, suffocating atmosphere. London is not just a backdrop — it is a Gothic space where truth is obscured, identities are hidden, and evil thrives in the gaps between respectability.

The fog serves a dual purpose. Literally, it obscures visibility — characters cannot see clearly, just as they cannot see the truth about Jekyll. Symbolically, it represents the moral fog of Victorian society, where appearances matter more than reality. When the fog lifts briefly during the Carew murder, the moonlight reveals the violence that normally remains hidden. Stevenson suggests that moments of clarity are rare and often horrifying.

Key Fact

Stevenson uses pathetic fallacy throughout the novella. Fog, darkness, wind, and shifting light mirror the characters’ psychological states and the moral darkness that pervades the story. When Utterson visits Hyde’s rooms in Soho after the Carew murder, the district is shrouded in a “great chocolate-coloured pall” of fog — the darkness of the setting reflects the darkness of Hyde’s actions.

The Door: Threshold Between Two Worlds

The sinister door in Chapter 1 is one of the novella’s most important symbols. It is “equipped with neither bell nor knocker” and is “blistered and distained.” It faces a busy street but belongs to a neglected, windowless wall. This door is the back entrance to Jekyll’s house — the entrance Hyde uses. The front of Jekyll’s house, on a respectable square, is grand and welcoming. The contrast is the novella in miniature: a polished public facade concealing a decaying, secret interior.

The door functions as a threshold between Jekyll’s public and private selves. When characters pass through it, they cross from the respectable world into the hidden one. Hyde enters and exits through this door; Jekyll never uses it publicly. The physical separation of the two entrances mirrors the psychological separation Jekyll attempts between his two identities — a separation that ultimately fails.

Jekyll’s cabinet — the private room connected to his laboratory — becomes his prison in the final chapters. He locks himself inside, refusing visitors, desperately trying to prevent Hyde from emerging in public. The locked door that once protected Jekyll’s secret now traps him. When Poole and Utterson break down the door with an axe, they are literally breaking through the barrier between the public and private worlds. What they find inside — Hyde’s body, not Jekyll’s — confirms that the secret has consumed the man who created it.

The cabinet also contains a mirror. Jekyll describes looking into it and seeing Hyde’s face staring back. The mirror is a classic Gothic motif — the doppelgänger confronting the self. The mirror forces Jekyll to acknowledge that Hyde is not someone else but a version of himself. This moment of recognition is central to the novella’s meaning: you cannot escape your own nature by giving it a different name.

Contrasting Spaces: Cavendish Square vs Soho

Stevenson uses London’s real geography to reinforce his themes. Jekyll’s house is in a wealthy, respectable area (loosely based on Cavendish Square). Hyde’s lodgings are in Soho — a district associated in the Victorian imagination with poverty, crime, and vice. The two addresses mirror Jekyll’s dual nature: the respectable doctor lives in the grand square, while his dark alter ego inhabits the dangerous slum.

When Utterson visits Hyde’s Soho rooms after the murder, he finds a disturbing mixture of luxury and squalor: good paintings, fine wine, and silver cutlery alongside ransacked drawers and a pile of burnt papers. Even Hyde’s private space reflects duality. The elegance comes from Jekyll’s taste; the chaos comes from Hyde’s nature. Stevenson reinforces the point that duality exists everywhere — not just within people but within the spaces they inhabit.

Narrative Structure: The Mystery Form

Stevenson structures the novella as a mystery with delayed revelation. For the first eight chapters, the reader shares Utterson’s perspective and investigates alongside him. The truth is not revealed until Chapters 9 and 10, in two embedded documents: Lanyon’s letter and Jekyll’s confession. This structure means the reader experiences the same shock of discovery as the characters — though modern readers usually know the twist in advance, the structure still shapes how we understand the themes.

Key Fact

Stevenson uses three narrative perspectives: third-person (Chapters 1–8, focused on Utterson), Lanyon’s first-person letter (Chapter 9), and Jekyll’s first-person confession (Chapter 10). Each narrator gets progressively closer to the truth but is also progressively more damaged by it. Utterson never fully understands; Lanyon understands but dies; Jekyll understands completely but is destroyed. The structure implies that complete knowledge of human duality is incompatible with survival.

The novella is full of documents that contain and control information: Jekyll’s will, Hyde’s forged letter, Lanyon’s sealed letter, and Jekyll’s full statement. These embedded narratives function as textual locked rooms. The truth is literally sealed away, only to be opened after death or disappearance. This mirrors Victorian society’s approach to uncomfortable truths: contain them, lock them up, and only confront them when there is no alternative. The sealed letters also create suspense — the reader knows that crucial information exists but must wait for it to be revealed.

Form: The Novella

Stevenson chose the novella form deliberately. At around 25,000 words, it is tightly compressed — there is no padding, no subplots, and very little description that does not serve the central theme. The brevity intensifies the claustrophobic atmosphere. Every detail matters: the description of a door, a hand, a piece of fog. Stevenson reportedly wrote the first draft in three days, then burned it and rewrote it in another three. The result is a narrative as concentrated and dangerous as Jekyll’s potion itself.

title: Chapters 9-10: The Revelations
content_html:
Chapter 9: Dr Lanyon’s Narrative

Stevenson finally delivers the confirmation. Lanyon’s sealed letter is a first-person account of a single terrible night. He receives a desperate note from Jekyll asking him to go to the cabinet and retrieve a drawer of chemicals. At midnight, a “small” stranger calls for the drawer. Lanyon describes him in now-familiar terms: “something abnormal and misbegotten… something seizing, surprising, and revolting.” This is the first time we meet Hyde through Lanyon’s professional, scientific eyes.

Key Fact

Stevenson withholds the transformation until Chapter 9 so that the reveal lands on a scientific, rational character (Lanyon) whom the reader has been taught to trust. The horror is not that Hyde changes — it is that a man of medicine watches it happen.

Hyde drinks the prepared potion. Lanyon describes what follows in stunned clauses: “he reeled, staggered, clutched at the table… and before my eyes — pale and shaken… there stood Henry Jekyll!” The dashes and staccato verbs mimic Lanyon’s shattered narration. Stevenson uses the sentence rhythm to stage the horror in real time.

Lanyon writes: “my life is shaken to its roots; sleep has left me… I cannot, even in my own thoughts, dwell on it without a start of horror.” The knowledge kills him — a direct echo of the Faust story, where the scholar who seeks forbidden knowledge is damned. Stevenson’s warning is moral: some truths are not survivable for those committed to empirical medicine.

Chapter 10: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case

The final chapter is Jekyll’s own long confession. Stevenson shifts voice entirely — the controlled, professional tone of Lanyon gives way to Jekyll’s restless self-examination. Jekyll explains that he was born with “duplicity of life”: a respectable surface and appetites “foreign” to it. He describes his scientific research and the creation of a drug that “could cast off the lower elements” of his personality.

The first transformation brings “incredibly sweet” freedom. As Hyde, Jekyll feels “younger, lighter, happier in body”, and experiences a “solution of the bonds of obligation.” Stevenson is careful: the freedom is pleasurable, which makes the moral warning more interesting. If evil felt only terrible, nobody would pursue it.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s central claim is that ‘man is not truly one, but truly two’. He believed he could separate the good and evil selves — but the evil, given its own body, grows stronger while the good weakens. The drug reveals the truth of duality but cannot manage it.

The Loss of Control

Gradually Jekyll loses the ability to return. After the Carew murder he vows never to take the drug again — but wakes in a park one morning as Hyde without taking it. Stevenson dramatises the addiction: Jekyll’s “powers seemed shaken”, the drug stops working reliably, and the original supply of the salt runs out. What saved him no longer exists. The final transformation is involuntary.

Jekyll’s confession ends with an extraordinary narrative move: he describes his own impending death in present tense. “This, then, is the last time… that Henry Jekyll can think his own thoughts or see his own face… in the glass.” Stevenson uses the last-words framing to make the reader complicit: we are reading a note that ends with the writer’s death.

Late-Victorian Britain was obsessed with doubles: the respectable husband who kept a mistress, the clergyman with a secret life, the civilised man who was also an animal. Stevenson crystallises this fear in one body. The novella was published in 1886, a year of high public tension about hidden vice, and the story became popular immediately. Jekyll’s confession reads like a Victorian nightmare turned inside out: the gentleman does the evil, not a stranger.

Modern criticism often reads Hyde as a figure for repressed Victorian sexuality, addiction, or class anxiety. Stevenson himself called the book ‘a fable’ — inviting interpretation. A strong essay treats the text as open to several readings rather than a puzzle with a single key.

Structure and Effect

Stevenson ends with a written confession because writing is what makes the story survivable. Jekyll’s words are preserved even as he dies; Utterson reads them and gains knowledge that Lanyon could not. The reader is a second Utterson, piecing the evidence into a whole. Structurally, the novella moves from street-level rumour to professional lawyer to scientific eyewitness to the subject’s own pen. Each stage gets closer to the truth — and each stage loses more of the person being described.

Why the Ending Matters

The ending is tragic rather than triumphant. There is no cure, no moral redemption, only a confession. Stevenson refuses the comfort of exorcism: Jekyll dies, Hyde dies, but the double remains as a lesson. The novella closes not with peace but with the reader’s new suspicion — of the doctors, gentlemen and lawyers who seemed so solid in Chapter 1.

title: Chapters 5-8: The Unravelling
content_html:
Chapter 5: After the Murder

After the Carew murder, Jekyll appears to reform. He resumes his charitable work, becomes sociable, and seems healthier. For two months, he avoids the potion and Hyde disappears. But Stevenson shows this apparent recovery is fragile. Jekyll has not conquered Hyde — he has simply stopped taking the drug. The desire remains. Jekyll describes the temptation as “the animal within me licking the chops of memory.” This metaphor is central: Hyde is not a separate creature but an appetite — a hunger that grows stronger the longer it is denied.

Then, sitting on a park bench in January, Jekyll transforms into Hyde without the potion. This is the novella’s most terrifying turning point. The transformation has become involuntary. Jekyll can no longer choose when to be Hyde — Hyde is asserting independence, growing stronger each time he is released. The power balance has shifted: “Hyde’s powers had grown with the sickliness of Jekyll.”

Key Fact

The involuntary transformation marks the point of no return. Jekyll can no longer control when Hyde appears. Stevenson uses this to argue that evil, once indulged, grows stronger: “Hyde’s powers had grown with the sickliness of Jekyll.” The relationship between Jekyll and Hyde has reversed — Hyde is now the dominant personality, and Jekyll is the one fighting for survival.

Chapter 6: Lanyon’s Decline

Dr Lanyon, once a healthy and jovial man, suddenly falls ill and dies within weeks. His decline is caused by something he has witnessed but refuses to discuss: “I have had a shock… and I shall never recover.” Stevenson withholds the details until Lanyon’s letter in Chapter 9, building suspense through gaps in information. Lanyon represents the rational, conventional Victorian mind: he cannot process what he has seen because it violates everything he believes about science and human nature.

Utterson and Enfield see Jekyll at an upstairs window. He begins to talk to them, then a look of “abject terror and despair” crosses his face and he slams the window shut. The two men walk away in horrified silence: “They were both pale; and there was an answering horror in their eyes.” Stevenson does not explain what happened — was Jekyll transforming? The reader is left to imagine, which is more disturbing than any explicit description.

The window scene is significant because it is the only time other characters witness Jekyll’s transformation (or near-transformation) in real time. The “answering horror” in Utterson and Enfield’s eyes suggests they have glimpsed something they cannot consciously acknowledge. Stevenson uses their silence as a metaphor for Victorian society’s refusal to confront the truths it already half-knows.

Chapter 8: The Last Night

Jekyll’s servant Poole arrives at Utterson’s door in a state of terror. He believes his master has been murdered because the voice coming from the locked laboratory sounds different: “That’s not Jekyll’s voice — it’s Hyde’s!” Utterson and Poole break down the door and find Hyde’s body, dead by suicide, still twitching, with a phial of poison in his hand. Jekyll is nowhere to be found. The suspense reaches its peak: where is Jekyll? The answer comes only in the final two chapters, through Lanyon’s narrative and Jekyll’s full statement.

The locked door of the laboratory is the novella’s most important symbol. It separates the known from the unknown, the public from the private, the respectable from the terrible. Throughout the story, characters approach this door but stop short of breaking it open — just as Victorian society approached uncomfortable truths but refused to confront them. When Utterson finally breaks it down, the mystery is resolved, but the cost is total: Jekyll is gone, Lanyon is dead, and the truth destroys the illusion of respectable normality.

The scene also uses Gothic tension: the servants huddled in the hallway, the strange voice behind the door, Poole’s whispered fear. Stevenson combines detective fiction with Gothic horror, making the reader both investigator and terrified witness.

Key Fact

The locked laboratory door symbolises Victorian secrecy — the refusal to confront uncomfortable truths. Characters approach but do not open it. When Utterson finally breaks it down, he discovers that Jekyll and Hyde are one person — that the respectable doctor and the savage murderer cannot be separated. The truth, once exposed, destroys everything.

title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
content_html:
Theme: Duality of Human Nature

The novella’s central argument is that every person contains both good and evil. Jekyll states: “man is not truly one, but truly two.” He attempts to separate these natures through science, but the experiment proves that they are inseparable. Hyde is not a foreign intruder but the part of Jekyll that society forced him to suppress. The novella argues that repression is more dangerous than acknowledgement: pretending evil does not exist makes it stronger, while recognising it honestly might allow it to be managed.

This theme connects to Victorian rationalism: the idea that civilised behaviour is a permanent achievement rather than a constant effort. Stevenson challenges this: civilisation is a thin veneer, and beneath it lies the same primitive nature that Darwin’s theory revealed. Hyde’s animalistic descriptions (“ape-like fury,” “troglodytic”) remind Victorian readers that evolution did not eliminate the animal — it only covered it with a suit and top hat.

Key Fact

Jekyll believes “man is not truly one, but truly two” and attempts to separate the two. But Stevenson’s novella shows this is impossible: good and evil are inseparable parts of the same person. Hyde cannot be permanently controlled or eliminated because he is Jekyll. The novella argues that managing duality requires honest self-knowledge, not scientific shortcuts.

Theme: Reputation and Secrecy

Every character in the novella guards his reputation obsessively. Jekyll hides Hyde behind a separate identity. Utterson refuses to gossip. Enfield’s rule is “the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask.” This culture of secrecy is presented as both symptom and cause of the problem: Victorian gentlemen cannot acknowledge their darker impulses because doing so would destroy their social standing. The result is that secrets fester, hidden selves grow stronger, and the eventual exposure is catastrophic.

Jekyll’s experiment represents science without ethical boundaries. He uses chemistry to achieve what nature forbids: the separation of good and evil. But the experiment is driven by selfish motives (freedom from moral accountability), and its consequences are disastrous. Stevenson was writing during a period of rapid scientific advance, and the novella warns that progress without morality leads to destruction.

Lanyon and Jekyll represent two attitudes to science: Lanyon is cautious and conventional, Jekyll is reckless and innovative. Both are inadequate. Stevenson suggests that science needs both ambition and restraint — a lesson that resonates far beyond the Victorian period.

Most 19th-century prose questions give you a printed extract and ask you to write about the extract and the novella as a whole. You will be assessed against the standard GCSE English Literature assessment objectives — AO1 (response with quotations), AO2 (language, form, structure), AO3 (context), and AO4 (written accuracy). Spend a few minutes annotating the extract before writing 4–5 developed paragraphs. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for exact mark weightings and timings.

Quotation bank: “Man is not truly one, but truly two” (duality). “The animal within me licking the chops of memory” (temptation). “With ape-like fury” (degeneration). “Deformity without nameable malformation” (indefinable evil). “Both sides were in dead earnest” (genuine duality). “I can be rid of Mr Hyde whenever I choose” (self-deception). Learn all six and practise linking each to multiple themes.

Connecting Themes

The genius of Jekyll and Hyde is that all themes connect. Duality drives the experiment, which raises questions about science and morality. The experiment must be kept secret because Victorian respectability cannot tolerate the truth about human nature. The secrecy enables Hyde’s crimes, which escalate because evil grows when indulged. The delayed revelation mirrors Victorian society’s refusal to confront what it already knows. In the exam, showing how themes interconnect demonstrates the sophisticated understanding that earns the highest marks.

Key Fact

The four main themes (duality, secrecy/reputation, science/morality, and the nature of evil) are interconnected: duality creates the desire for separation, the experiment requires secrecy, secrecy enables escalation, and escalation proves that evil cannot be controlled. Showing these connections in the exam demonstrates whole-text understanding.

title: Character Analysis
content_html:
Dr Jekyll: The Divided Self

Dr Henry Jekyll is a “large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty,” respected, wealthy, and apparently moral. But in his ‘Full Statement of the Case’ he confesses: “I concealed my pleasures; and when I reached years of reflection… I stood already committed to a profound duplicity of life.” Jekyll has always been divided. His experiment does not create Hyde — it releases a self that was already there.

Jekyll’s tragedy is that he wants to have it both ways: to enjoy ‘pleasures’ while maintaining his reputation. The potion initially seems to offer this. He can be Hyde at night and Jekyll by day. But the balance shifts. Hyde grows stronger; Jekyll grows weaker. The transformations begin happening involuntarily. Jekyll discovers too late that you cannot neatly separate good from evil — they are intertwined. As he puts it: “All human beings… are commingled out of good and evil.”

Key Fact

Jekyll’s ‘profound duplicity’ existed before the potion. He always concealed his desires behind respectability. The experiment simply makes the duality physical. His tragedy: trying to separate good from evil destroys both — ‘all human beings are commingled out of good and evil.’

Mr Hyde: The Primitive Self

Hyde is physically smaller, younger, and uglier than Jekyll. Everyone who encounters him feels instinctive revulsion but cannot explain why. Enfield describes “something wrong with his appearance; something displeasing, something downright detestable.” This indefinable repulsion is deliberate: Stevenson suggests that evil is felt rather than understood, sensed on a primal level.

Hyde’s violence escalates through the novella. He tramples a child in Chapter 1 and murders Sir Danvers Carew with a cane in Chapter 4, beating him with “ape-like fury.” He is “like a monkey” and moves with “extraordinary quickness.” The animalistic language connects Hyde to post-Darwinian fears about the beast within. He represents what Jekyll’s repression has created: a creature of pure appetite, without conscience or restraint.

Jekyll explains that Hyde is smaller because evil has been “less exercised and much less exhausted” in his life. Jekyll has spent decades developing his good side while repressing his evil. Hyde is stunted because he has had less opportunity to grow. This detail reinforces the theme of repression: the evil side is smaller because it has been compressed, not eliminated. And when it finally emerges, it does so with concentrated, explosive force.

Utterson: The Reliable Witness

Gabriel John Utterson is Jekyll’s lawyer, friend, and the novella’s primary narrator. He is described as “lean, cold, scanty, and yet somehow lovable.” Utterson represents Victorian propriety at its best: loyal, discreet, non-judgemental. He suspects something terrible but never pries too aggressively. His restraint reflects the Victorian code that demanded respect for privacy — but also makes him complicit in concealment.

Utterson is the reader’s guide through the mystery. His limited perspective creates suspense: he sees the external evidence (the door, the will, Hyde’s behaviour) without understanding the truth. Stevenson uses Utterson to show how Victorian respectability prevented people from confronting uncomfortable truths. Utterson’s decency is genuine, but his deference to social convention means he cannot save his friend.

Key Fact

Utterson embodies the best of Victorian propriety: loyal, discreet, non-judgemental. But his respect for privacy and convention prevents him from investigating aggressively enough to save Jekyll. Stevenson shows that the very decency of Victorian culture can enable concealment and tragedy.

Dr Lanyon: The Shock of Truth

Dr Lanyon is Jekyll’s old friend and a conventional scientist who dismissed Jekyll’s experiments as “unscientific balderdash.” When he witnesses Hyde’s transformation into Jekyll, the shock kills him. Lanyon represents the Victorian worldview that cannot accommodate the truth about human nature. Faced with evidence that good and evil coexist within one person, he literally cannot survive the knowledge.

Richard Enfield, Utterson’s kinsman, witnesses Hyde trampling a child. His response is telling: he does not report it to the police but instead forces Hyde to pay compensation. This ‘gentleman’s agreement’ to resolve the matter privately, avoiding scandal, is pure Victorian respectability. Enfield and Utterson later agree never to discuss the matter again: “Let us make a bargain never to refer to this again.” Stevenson shows how Victorian discretion actively suppresses truth.

title: Chapters 1-4: Mystery and Terror
content_html:
Chapter 1: The Story of the Door

The novella opens with Mr Utterson and his cousin Richard Enfield taking their regular Sunday walk. They pass a sinister door in a side street — “the door, which was equipped with neither bell nor knocker.” This door is the back entrance to Dr Jekyll’s house, and it immediately establishes the novella’s central symbol: a boundary between the respectable and the hidden, the public and the private.

Enfield tells Utterson about a disturbing incident he witnessed. Late one night, he saw a small, deformed man trample over a young girl at a street corner. The man showed no remorse. Enfield and a doctor confronted the man, who calmly went through the sinister door and returned with a cheque signed by a reputable person — Dr Jekyll. The attacker was Edward Hyde.

Key Fact

Hyde’s trampling of the girl is the novella’s first act of violence. Enfield describes it with horror: Hyde was “like some damned Juggernaut” — an unstoppable, inhuman force. The victim is a child, making Hyde’s callousness especially shocking. Stevenson uses this scene to establish Hyde as someone who inspires instinctive disgust before any explanation is given.

Chapter 2: Search for Mr Hyde

Utterson is deeply troubled by Enfield’s story, particularly because he is Jekyll’s lawyer and has recently read Jekyll’s will. The will states that in the event of Jekyll’s “disappearance or unexplained absence,” all his possessions should pass to Edward Hyde. Utterson suspects blackmail — that Hyde has some dark secret about Jekyll and is using it to extort money and the inheritance.

Utterson declares: “If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek.” This pun reveals Utterson’s determination to investigate, but also establishes the detective-story structure of the novella. The reader, like Utterson, is drawn into the mystery of Hyde’s identity and his connection to Jekyll. Stevenson withholds the truth until the final two chapters, building suspense through delayed revelation.

When Utterson finally meets Hyde outside the sinister door, he is repelled. Hyde gives “an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation.” Nobody can describe exactly what is wrong with Hyde’s appearance, yet everyone who sees him feels an instinctive revulsion. Enfield earlier described “Satan’s signature upon a face.” Stevenson deliberately makes Hyde’s horror indefinable — this is more unsettling than a specific deformity because it suggests something fundamentally wrong at the level of the soul.

Every character who encounters Hyde struggles to articulate what makes him so disturbing. Enfield says he is “not easy to describe” and that there is “something wrong with his appearance; something displeasing, something downright detestable.” Utterson notes “an impression of deformity” without being able to name the specific defect. This technique serves Stevenson’s purpose brilliantly: if Hyde’s evil were visible in a simple way (a scar, a limp), the reader could contain and categorise it. By making the horror ineffable, Stevenson implies that Hyde’s wrongness is spiritual rather than physical — and that recognising evil is an instinct, not a rational observation.

Chapter 3: Dr Jekyll Was Quite at Ease

Utterson visits Jekyll to voice his concerns about the will. Jekyll dismisses Utterson’s fears, insisting: “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde.” This is dramatic irony — the reader eventually discovers that Jekyll will lose precisely this power. Jekyll asks Utterson to promise that he will carry out the terms of the will if anything happens. Utterson reluctantly agrees, bound by professional duty and personal loyalty.

At this point, Jekyll appears calm, in control, and entirely the respectable Victorian gentleman. The contrast with what comes later makes this chapter essential for understanding Jekyll’s tragic arc: he genuinely believes he can manage the situation. His confidence is his hubris.

Chapter 4: The Carew Murder Case

Eight months later, Hyde commits a far more terrible crime. A maidservant witnesses the murder of Sir Danvers Carew from her window. She describes how Carew — an elderly, white-haired gentleman — politely addressed a small man she recognised as Hyde. Without provocation, Hyde attacked Carew with “ape-like fury,” beating him to death with a heavy cane and stamping on the body. The cane broke in two under the force of the blows.

Key Fact

The Carew murder is a turning point. Hyde’s violence has escalated from trampling a child to beating an elderly man to death. The phrase “ape-like fury” connects Hyde to animalistic regression and Darwinian fears. Sir Danvers Carew was a Member of Parliament — Hyde’s victim is not just any person but a pillar of the establishment, making the crime an attack on respectable society itself.

The maidservant is one of only two women in the entire novella (the other is the girl Hyde tramples). She watches the murder from a window “romantically given” and by the light of a full moon. Her perspective is emotional and atmospheric — she describes the scene as beautiful before it turns horrific. Stevenson uses her viewpoint to create a dreamlike quality that intensifies the horror. The maid faints after watching the murder, recovering only to call the police. Her marginality in the story reflects the novella’s focus on the exclusively male world of Victorian professional life — a world where women are either victims or peripheral witnesses.

After the murder, Utterson takes the police to Hyde’s rooms in Soho. The contrast is striking: half the rooms are furnished with luxury and good taste, while the other half are in disarray, with clothes thrown on the floor and a pile of ash in the fireplace where Hyde has been burning papers. Even Hyde’s lodgings reflect the duality at the heart of the novella — elegance and chaos existing in the same space.

title: Context: Victorian Society and Duality
content_html:
Why Context Matters

To understand The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, you need to understand the world Robert Louis Stevenson was writing in. The novella was published in 1886, during the height of the Victorian era. Victorian society shaped every character, theme and plot twist in the story.

Victorian Respectability

The Victorians placed enormous value on respectability. For middle- and upper-class men like Jekyll, Utterson and Enfield, reputation was everything. A gentleman was expected to be moral, restrained and rational at all times. Any sign of improper behaviour — gambling, drinking, sexual misconduct — could destroy a man’s standing in society.

This obsession with appearances created a culture of hypocrisy. Many Victorians lived double lives: respectable in public, indulgent in private. Stevenson’s novella directly explores this idea through Jekyll’s transformation into Hyde.

Key Fact

Victorian London had a stark divide between the wealthy West End and the poverty-stricken East End. Stevenson uses settings like Soho to represent the hidden, darker side of respectable society.

Science and Darwin

The Victorian period saw extraordinary scientific progress. Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, arguing that humans had evolved from animals. This was deeply shocking to a society built on Christian beliefs. If humans were just advanced animals, perhaps the “beast” was still inside them.

Stevenson taps into this fear. Hyde is described in animalistic terms — “like a monkey,” “troglodytic.” Jekyll’s experiment suggests that the primitive, violent side of human nature can never be fully suppressed, only hidden behind a mask of civilisation.

Degeneration theory was a popular Victorian idea that humanity could evolve backwards. Scientists feared that immoral behaviour, poverty and disease could cause people to regress into primitive creatures. Hyde embodies this fear — he is smaller, younger and more ape-like than Jekyll, as though he represents an earlier, less evolved version of humanity.

Religion and Morality

Victorian Britain was deeply religious. The Church taught that good and evil were separate forces, and that moral people could resist sin through willpower and faith. Jekyll’s experiment challenges this: it suggests that evil is not external but lives inside every person.

This would have horrified Victorian readers. The idea that a respectable doctor could harbour murderous impulses struck at the heart of their moral framework.

Key Fact

Stevenson was raised in a strict Calvinist household in Edinburgh. Calvinism taught that humans are born sinful, which directly influenced the novella’s exploration of innate evil.

Gothic literature was hugely popular in the Victorian era. Writers like Mary Shelley (Frankenstein) and Bram Stoker (Dracula) explored fears about science, morality and the unknown. Stevenson’s novella fits squarely in the Gothic tradition: it features a mad scientist, a monstrous double, dark London streets and an atmosphere of creeping dread.

The Gothic genre allowed Victorian writers to explore taboo subjects — violence, desire, madness — in a way that “respectable” fiction could not.

Stevenson’s Life

Robert Louis Stevenson was born in Edinburgh in 1850. Edinburgh itself was a city of contrasts: the elegant, respectable New Town and the dark, crowded Old Town existed side by side. This real-life duality influenced the novella’s exploration of hidden identities.

Stevenson reportedly wrote the first draft of the novella in just three days after a vivid nightmare. His wife Fanny criticised the draft for being too much of a straightforward horror story, so he burned it and rewrote it as an allegory about the duality of human nature.

Stevenson was fascinated by the real-life story of Deacon Brodie, an 18th-century Edinburgh cabinet-maker who was a respected citizen by day and a burglar by night. Brodie was eventually caught and executed. Stevenson even co-wrote a play about him. The parallels with Jekyll and Hyde are obvious — Brodie was a real-life example of Victorian duality.

title: Setting & Narrative
content_html:
London: A City of Duality

Stevenson’s London is both real and symbolic. The city’s geography mirrors Jekyll’s duality: respectable streets sit next to squalid alleys; wealth borders poverty; daylight gives way to fog and darkness. The fog is described as “a great chocolate-coloured pall” that descends over the city, obscuring vision and blurring boundaries. When Utterson walks through London at night, “the fog settled down upon that part, as brown as umber” — Stevenson uses pathetic fallacy to show that moral clarity is impossible in this world of concealment.

The contrast between day and night is central. By day, London’s streets are busy and respectable. By night, they become threatening and strange. Hyde operates at night; Jekyll maintains his reputation by day. The city itself has a dual identity.

Key Fact

London’s fog symbolises moral confusion and concealment. The city’s day/night contrast mirrors Jekyll/Hyde’s duality. Respectable streets border squalid alleys. The setting is not just background — it embodies the novella’s central theme.

The House with Two Faces

Jekyll’s house is the novella’s most powerful symbol. The front faces a respectable square: “a certain sinister block of building” with “a great air of wealth and comfort.” But the back, facing a by-street, has a door that is “blistered and distained” with “neither bell nor knocker.” Hyde enters and exits through this back door. The house IS Jekyll’s duality made physical: a respectable front concealing a degraded rear.

Stevenson develops this symbolism throughout. Jekyll’s laboratory — where the transformations occur — is at the back of the house, hidden from view. The front rooms are elegant; the laboratory is described as a “dismal” former dissecting theatre. The architecture maps perfectly onto the theme: the pleasant, public rooms of Jekyll’s respectable life conceal the dark, private space where Hyde is created.

Doors and windows recur throughout the novella. The back door has no bell or knocker — it is designed for secret access. Jekyll’s window, from which Utterson and Enfield see him, is the threshold between his public and private selves: when they catch him there, his expression changes to one of “abject terror and despair.” The final scene involves Poole and Utterson breaking down Jekyll’s cabinet door — literally forcing open the space of concealment. Stevenson uses doors as structural metaphors for the barriers between public respectability and private truth.

Narrative Structure: The Mystery Unveiled

The novella uses a complex narrative structure with multiple perspectives. The first eight chapters follow Utterson’s investigation. Chapter 9 is Dr Lanyon’s narrative. Chapter 10 is ‘Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case.’ Each narrator sees only part of the truth; only when combined do they reveal the whole picture.

This structure serves several purposes. It creates suspense (the reader discovers the truth alongside Utterson). It mirrors the theme of concealment (the truth is literally buried in sealed documents). And it suggests that identity is never fully knowable from any single perspective. Stevenson tells us that even our closest friends may be strangers to us.

Key Fact

Three narrators: Utterson sees external evidence but not the truth; Lanyon witnesses the transformation and dies; Jekyll provides the full interior confession. Each perspective is partial. Only together do they reveal the whole story. This mirrors Victorian society’s fragmented understanding of the self.

Sealed Documents and Delayed Revelation

The truth about Jekyll and Hyde is contained in sealed documents: Jekyll’s will (which puzzles Utterson from the start), Lanyon’s letter (marked ‘not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr Henry Jekyll’), and Jekyll’s own statement. These sealed documents are a structural metaphor for repression: truth exists but is locked away, only to be released when concealment is no longer possible.

The novella’s final chapter — Jekyll’s statement — shifts from third-person mystery to first-person confession. This change in narrative voice forces the reader into Jekyll’s mind, creating uncomfortable intimacy with a man who has done terrible things. Stevenson wants us to understand Jekyll’s perspective, not just judge it.

The novella ends with Jekyll’s statement, not with Utterson’s reaction. There is no neat conclusion, no moral summary, no reassurance. Jekyll’s final words — “Here then, as I lay down the pen and proceed to seal up my confession, I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end” — leave us with his voice, his despair, and no comfort. Stevenson refuses to tidy up the horror. The reader must sit with the implications: that duality is universal, that repression creates monsters, and that no one can truly know another person.

title: Chapters 1-4: Mystery & Terror
content_html:
Chapter 1: The Story of the Door

Stevenson opens with the lawyer Mr Utterson and his cousin Enfield walking in a “by-street” in London. The contrast is deliberate: the street is well-kept, “clean”, lively — except for one “sinister” building with “a blistered and distained” door. Stevenson uses the Gothic technique of the uncanny: a single wrong detail in an ordinary scene makes the reader suspicious of everything around it.

Key Fact

The neglected door is Stevenson’s first symbol of duality. Opening the novella with a building rather than a person signals that the whole story will be about hidden rooms — literal and psychological.

Enfield tells the story of a “small man” who “trampled calmly” over a young girl and gave him “a look so ugly it brought out the sweat on me like running.” The repeated word “trample” stays with the reader — the violence is described less in physical detail than in the witnesses’ reactions. Stevenson uses this reflected horror to make Hyde feel more disturbing than any explicit description could.

Chapter 2: Search for Mr Hyde

Utterson, disturbed by the story, reads Jekyll’s will: on Jekyll’s death or “disappearance” of more than three months, everything is to go to “Edward Hyde.” The legal language — precise, formal — makes the strangeness worse. Utterson begins to dream of Hyde “crushing” children, then sets out to hunt him by the door on Bye Street.

When they finally meet, Hyde is described in strikingly unstable terms. Utterson says: “God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic, shall we say?… he gives a strong feeling of deformity, although I couldn’t specify the point.” Stevenson deliberately refuses detail. Hyde is felt rather than seen. This indirect characterisation echoes Victorian anxieties about degeneration and the unspeakable inside the respectable.

Stevenson puns on Utterson’s name (“he will be Mr Seek”) and on Hyde’s (“to hide”). The playfulness is deliberate: under the surface of every Victorian gentleman is something hidden. Stevenson was writing in 1886, the year after W. T. Stead’s “Maiden Tribute” exposé revealed widespread sexual exploitation by respectable London men. The theme of public respectability concealing private vice was everywhere.

Chapter 3: Dr Jekyll was Quite at Ease

Two weeks later Utterson dines at Jekyll’s and raises the will. Jekyll’s refusal is polite but final: “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde.” The claim is the first lie. Stevenson lets the reader hear it as confident reassurance and only later realise it is false. Utterson is presented as the rational Victorian gentleman — lawyer, discreet, loyal — the kind of man readers were invited to trust with the story.

Chapter 4: The Carew Murder Case

The novella’s first moment of clear violence comes with Sir Danvers Carew’s murder. A servant girl watches from a moonlit window as Carew is “trampled” and “clubbed… with ape-like fury” by Hyde. Stevenson’s simile — “ape-like” — draws on Victorian degeneration theories. Darwin’s Descent of Man (1871) had shaken confidence that humans were truly separate from animals.

The setting amplifies the horror: a full moon, a silent street, a respected MP killed for no reason. Stevenson chooses the victim carefully. Carew is an “aged” gentleman with “silvery hair” — the symbol of Victorian respectability. Hyde’s violence is not crime but sacrilege.

Key Fact

Stevenson uses three key phrases in the Carew murder: ‘trampled’, ‘ape-like fury’ and ‘bones were audibly shattered’. Each word strips away civilised language and pushes Hyde closer to the animal.

Stevenson builds these chapters through embedded narration: Enfield tells Utterson, who reads the will, who hears Poole, who hears the maid. No one has the whole story. The readers have to assemble it — a deliberate technique that mirrors the novella’s theme: nothing is as single or stable as it appears.

The delayed revelation is also a narrative suspense machine. We suspect a link between Jekyll and Hyde long before it is confirmed. Stevenson’s 1886 readers, reading the novella in a small red shilling edition, would have experienced this as a shock. Modern readers, knowing the twist, can analyse how the structure creates the possibility of that shock.

Why These Chapters Matter

The first four chapters teach the reader how to read the whole novella. Stevenson trains us to distrust surfaces: the tidy street with one wrong door; the respectable Jekyll with one dubious beneficiary; the quiet night with a moonlit murder. The doubling that will later be explicit is already present in the structure.

title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
content_html:
Theme 1: Duality of Human Nature

The central theme of the novella is expressed in Jekyll’s declaration: “Man is not truly one, but truly two.” Stevenson argues that every person contains both good and evil impulses. Victorian society demanded that people suppress their darker urges and present a unified, moral exterior. Jekyll’s experiment is an attempt to resolve this tension by literally dividing himself into two separate beings. It fails catastrophically because evil, once released, cannot be contained.

The theme of duality extends beyond Jekyll himself. London is divided between wealthy squares and squalid slums. Jekyll’s house has a grand front and a sinister back. The novella’s structure is split between investigation and confession. Even minor characters display duality: Utterson suppresses his own pleasures, and Enfield lives a double social life. Stevenson’s message is universal: duality is not Jekyll’s personal pathology but the human condition.

Key Fact

Stevenson does not present Jekyll as uniquely evil. Jekyll confesses: “I learned to recognise the thorough and primitive duality of man.” The word “man” is universal — this applies to all people, not just Jekyll. The novella’s horror is not that one man has a dark side, but that everyone does. The Victorian pretence that respectability equals goodness is the real delusion Stevenson attacks.

Theme 2: Repression and Its Consequences

Repression is both the cause and the catastrophe of the novella. Jekyll does not create Hyde because he is unusually wicked — he creates Hyde because Victorian society forces him to bury all his “undignified” desires. The pressure to appear perpetually virtuous is what drives him to seek a scientific escape. Stevenson implies that repression does not eliminate dangerous urges; it stores them up until they explode with greater violence.

Hyde’s escalating brutality — from trampling a girl to murdering Sir Danvers Carew — demonstrates this principle. Each act of indulgence does not satisfy Hyde’s desires but intensifies them. Jekyll describes a “leap of welcome” with each transformation, the language of addiction. Stevenson’s warning is clear: a society built on repression breeds monsters, because the desires it forces underground do not disappear — they grow.

The novella is obsessed with secrets. Every major character keeps them: Jekyll hides his experiment, Lanyon seals his letter, Utterson refuses to speak about what he has seen at the window, Enfield agrees never to discuss the trampling incident. Reputation is the currency of Victorian professional life, and every character works to protect it — sometimes at the cost of truth and safety.

This culture of secrecy enables Jekyll’s double life. Nobody investigates too closely because doing so would risk exposing uncomfortable truths — not just about Jekyll, but about the entire class of respectable gentlemen. Utterson suspects blackmail because it is a socially understandable crime; the actual truth (one person containing two identities) is too threatening to the Victorian worldview to even consider. Stevenson suggests that Victorian society’s commitment to reputation creates a system where dangerous secrets are not just tolerated but actively protected.

Theme 3: Science and Morality

Jekyll’s experiment raises profound questions about the limits of science. He uses chemistry to divide the human soul — an act that crosses the boundary between science and the sacred. His creation of Hyde echoes the overreaching scientist of Gothic tradition — most obviously Victor Frankenstein, who also creates a monster by transgressing natural boundaries.

Lanyon represents the opposing view: cautious, conventional science that stays within accepted limits. He dismisses Jekyll’s work as “unscientific balderdash.” Yet Lanyon is also destroyed — not by his own experiment but by witnessing Jekyll’s. Stevenson implies that there is no safe position in the science-versus-morality debate: pushing too far is fatal, but so is being confronted by someone else’s transgression. The novella was published in the same decade as Darwin’s legacy debates and the rise of experimental medicine, making its anxiety about science’s moral limits sharply topical.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s experiment fails not because of a scientific error but because of a moral miscalculation. He assumed evil could be separated and contained. Instead, it grows stronger when given freedom. The impure chemical that made the experiment possible cannot be reproduced, suggesting that the transformation was partly accidental — Jekyll never fully understood what he was doing. Stevenson presents scientific ambition without moral restraint as inherently dangerous.

Theme 4: Violence and the Primitive Self

Hyde’s violence is described in animalistic terms: “ape-like fury,” “troglodyte,” and other language that connects him to atavism. This reflects the post-Darwinian anxiety that beneath civilised behaviour, humans remain animals capable of savage violence. Hyde is physically smaller than Jekyll, suggesting the primitive self is normally kept small by social constraint. As Hyde is indulged, he grows — both in physical stature and in dominance over Jekyll’s consciousness.

Extract-based analysis: Questions on the novella often begin by giving you a printed extract of around 400 words. Focus on language analysis: individual words, phrases, imagery, sentence structure. Use the PEA/PEEL framework but go deeper: what does this specific word choice reveal? What effect does it have on the reader? How does it connect to Stevenson’s wider purpose? Allow yourself enough time to produce three or four developed paragraphs rather than rushing through six superficial ones — check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact timing.

Whole-text response: Most exam questions also require you to explore a theme, character, or idea across the novella as a whole. Range confidently across the text, using memorised quotations from at least three or four different chapters. Structure your response thematically, not chronologically. For example, for a question on duality, you might discuss: the physical duality of Jekyll/Hyde, the geographical duality of London, the structural duality of the narrative, and the psychological duality within all the characters. Each point should be supported by a short, precise quotation.

Closed book strategy: Most GCSE literature papers are closed book, so memorise 10–15 key quotations that cover the major themes and characters. Short quotations (3–6 words) are best: “ape-like fury,” “Satan’s signature,” “not truly one, but truly two,” “slowly losing hold.” Each quotation should be versatile enough to use for multiple questions. Always analyse the specific language of the quotation — do not simply drop it in as evidence without comment.

Key Quotation Bank

The following quotations are the most important to memorise for the exam. Each one connects to multiple themes:

Jekyll

“Man is not truly one, but truly two”

The novella’s thesis: duality is universal, not personal.

Utterson

“If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek”

The detective narrative begins. Utterson’s rational approach to an irrational mystery.

Narrator

“Ape-like fury”

Hyde’s violence. Darwinian regression. The primitive self unleashed.

Enfield

“Satan’s signature upon a face”

Hyde’s evil is instinctively recognised but rationally indescribable.

Jekyll

“I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self”

The loss of control. Evil grows when indulged. Addiction and despair.

Setting

“The fog still slept on the wing above the drowned city”

Gothic atmosphere. London as a character. Concealment and moral obscurity.

Setting

“The door, which was equipped with neither bell nor knocker”

The threshold between public and private. Repulsion. Secrecy.

title: Chapters 7–10: The Last Night and Jekyll’s Statement
content_html:
Chapter 7: Incident at the Window

Utterson and Enfield pass Jekyll’s house and see him sitting at an upstairs window, looking “like some disconsolate prisoner.” They exchange pleasantries, and for a moment Jekyll seems to relax. Then, suddenly, a look of terror crosses his face, and he slams the window shut.

Utterson and Enfield walk away in silence, both deeply shaken. Stevenson never explains what happened at the window — the reader must infer that Jekyll was beginning to transform into Hyde involuntarily. This is the novella’s most chilling moment of withholding.

Key Fact

The window scene mirrors the opening “door” scene. Both involve Utterson and Enfield witnessing something disturbing connected to Jekyll’s house, and both end with a silent agreement not to discuss it. This structural echo reinforces the theme of Victorian repression.

Chapter 8: The Last Night

Jekyll’s butler Poole comes to Utterson in a state of panic. He believes his master has been murdered and replaced by someone hiding in the laboratory. Poole says the voice behind the locked door no longer sounds like Jekyll — it sounds like Hyde.

Utterson and Poole break down the door with an axe. Inside, they find Hyde’s body on the floor, dressed in Jekyll’s clothes, which are “far too large for him.” He has taken poison. Jekyll is nowhere to be found.

This chapter is the novella’s climax. Stevenson builds tension through Gothic elements: the screaming wind, the silent servants gathered in the hall, the sounds of pacing behind the locked door. The axe breaking down the door symbolises the violent exposure of Jekyll’s secret — the barriers he built between his public and private selves are literally smashed apart.

Finding Hyde in Jekyll’s oversized clothes provides the final physical clue. Hyde is smaller because he represents the part of Jekyll that was suppressed and undeveloped — his evil side had less “exercise” than his good side.

Chapter 9: Dr Lanyon’s Narrative

The narrative shifts from third-person to Lanyon’s own account, contained in his sealed letter. Lanyon describes receiving a desperate letter from Jekyll, asking him to collect chemicals from the laboratory and give them to a stranger who would arrive at midnight.

The stranger turns out to be Hyde. In front of Lanyon, Hyde drinks the potion and transforms back into Jekyll. Lanyon is so horrified that his health collapses — this is the “shock” he mentioned in Chapter 6.

Key Fact

The shift to Lanyon’s first-person narrative is structurally significant. It moves the reader from Utterson’s limited, rational perspective to the direct testimony of someone who witnessed the impossible. This makes the supernatural element feel more real and immediate.

Chapter 10: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case

The final chapter is Jekyll’s own confession. He explains that he had always felt a duality within himself — a respectable public self and a hidden, pleasure-seeking private self. His experiment was designed to separate these two natures.

At first, Jekyll enjoyed the freedom of being Hyde. As Hyde, he could indulge in “undignified” pleasures without risking his reputation. But over time, Hyde grew stronger and more violent, while Jekyll grew weaker. Eventually, the transformations began happening involuntarily — Jekyll would wake up as Hyde without having taken the potion.

“Man is not truly one, but truly two” — Jekyll’s central insight, challenging the Victorian belief that identity is fixed and unified.

“I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self, and becoming slowly incorporated with my second and worse” — shows that evil, once indulged, takes over.

“It was Hyde, after all, and Hyde alone, that was guilty” — Jekyll tries to distance himself from responsibility, but the reader recognises this as self-deception.

The novella uses three different narrators: the third-person account focused on Utterson (Chapters 1–8), Lanyon’s first-person letter (Chapter 9), and Jekyll’s first-person confession (Chapter 10). Each narrator sees more of the truth than the last. This layered structure mirrors the peeling away of Jekyll’s disguise — the deeper we go, the closer we get to the horrifying reality.

title: Characters: Utterson, Lanyon and Enfield
content_html:
Mr Gabriel John Utterson

Utterson is the novella’s main focaliser for Chapters 1–8. He is a lawyer: rational, loyal and deeply private. Stevenson introduces him as a man of “rugged countenance” who is “lean, long, dusty, dreary” but somehow still “lovable.”

Utterson embodies Victorian respectability. He suppresses his own desires — he enjoys the theatre but has not been to one in twenty years. He drinks gin to “mortify a taste for vintages” (punishing himself for enjoying good wine). He tolerates the failings of others without judging them, preferring to maintain social harmony.

Key Fact

Utterson is a mirror of Jekyll — both repress their desires, but Utterson does so without catastrophic consequences. He represents what Jekyll could have been if he had accepted his limitations rather than trying to transcend them.

Utterson functions as a detective figure. He stakes out Hyde, examines the will, questions Lanyon and eventually breaks down Jekyll’s door. But his Victorian propriety limits his effectiveness — he refuses to open Lanyon’s sealed letter, avoids prying into Jekyll’s private life, and consistently chooses discretion over truth.

This makes Utterson both sympathetic and frustrating. The reader can see clues that Utterson misses or deliberately ignores. Stevenson uses this gap between what the reader suspects and what Utterson knows to build dramatic irony.

Dr Hastie Lanyon

Lanyon is an old friend of Jekyll’s and a fellow doctor. He is described as “hearty, healthy, dapper” and full of confidence. He represents orthodox science — rational, empirical and cautious.

Lanyon dismisses Jekyll’s experiments as “unscientific balderdash.” This disagreement ended their friendship years before the novella begins. When Lanyon finally witnesses Hyde’s transformation into Jekyll, the shock destroys him — he dies within weeks.

Key Fact

Lanyon’s death shows the danger of confronting truths that a person is not prepared for. His rational worldview cannot accommodate what he has seen. Stevenson suggests that some knowledge is too terrible for the human mind to bear — a classic Gothic theme.

Lanyon represents the Victorian scientific establishment — cautious, evidence-based and respectable. Jekyll represents the maverick scientist who pushes beyond accepted boundaries. Their disagreement mirrors real Victorian debates about the limits of science, particularly after Darwin’s theory of evolution challenged religious certainties.

Stevenson does not clearly side with either. Lanyon’s caution is admirable but ultimately leads to ignorance. Jekyll’s ambition is intellectually bold but morally reckless. Both approaches fail.

Richard Enfield

Enfield is Utterson’s cousin and walking companion. He is described as a “well-known man about town” — sociable, worldly and less restrained than Utterson. It is Enfield who tells the story of Hyde trampling the girl in Chapter 1, setting the plot in motion.

Despite being more open than Utterson, Enfield shares the same commitment to discretion. After telling the trampling story, he immediately suggests: “let us make a bargain never to refer to this again.” This instinct to suppress uncomfortable knowledge is central to the novella’s critique of Victorian society.

Poole (Jekyll’s butler) represents the servant class. His loyalty to Jekyll drives the climactic break-in scene. His willingness to act when his master is in danger contrasts with Utterson’s cautious hesitation.

Mr Guest (Utterson’s clerk) notices the matching handwriting. His observational skill as a professional handwriting analyst advances the plot where Utterson’s propriety would not.

The maid who witnesses the Carew murder is one of very few female characters. Her emotional, swooning response contrasts with the male characters’ restraint, reflecting Victorian gender expectations.

title: Chapters 9-10: The Revelations
content_html:
Chapter 9: Dr Lanyon’s Narrative

Lanyon’s letter, opened after his death, reveals what killed him. Jekyll (as Hyde) sent Lanyon instructions to collect chemicals from the laboratory. When Lanyon witnesses Hyde drink the potion and transform into Jekyll before his eyes, the shock destroys him: “My life is shaken to its roots; sleep has left me; the deadliest terror sits by me at all hours.” Lanyon’s testimony gives the reader the first direct description of the transformation — and confirms that Jekyll and Hyde are the same person.

Stevenson delays this revelation until Chapter 9 of 10 — a structural choice that maximises impact. The reader has spent eight chapters constructing theories (blackmail? murder? a secret relative?), and the truth is more disturbing than any of them. Lanyon’s horror is not just at the physical transformation but at its implications: if a respectable doctor contains a murderer, what might anyone contain? The truth about duality is literally lethal to the Victorian mind.

Key Fact

Stevenson delays the truth until Chapter 9, making the reader experience the same process of discovery as the characters. This delayed revelation maximises shock: eight chapters of mystery resolve into a truth more disturbing than any theory. Lanyon’s death proves that the Victorian world cannot survive the knowledge of its own duality.

Chapter 10: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case

Jekyll’s confession is the novella’s final chapter and its richest for analysis. He describes his life before the experiment: “I was in no sense a hypocrite; both sides of me were in dead earnest.” He was genuinely good and genuinely drawn to vice. The experiment did not create evil — it separated it from the restraints of conscience. Hyde was “pure evil” because he was Jekyll without the moral part: “Edward Hyde, alone in the ranks of mankind, was pure evil.”

Jekyll describes his initial pleasure in being Hyde: “I felt younger, lighter, happier in body… I knew myself, at the first breath of this new life, to be more wicked, tenfold more wicked… and the thought, in that moment, braced and delighted me like wine.” The language of pleasure and intoxication (“lighter,” “delighted,” “wine”) reveals that Jekyll enjoyed being Hyde. He does not present himself as a victim of his experiment but as someone who chose to indulge his darkest impulses and found it addictive.

Hyde is smaller than Jekyll because, as Jekyll explains, “the evil side of my nature… was less robust and less developed than the good.” This is because Jekyll had spent his life exercising virtue and suppressing vice. But once released, evil grows: “I began to be tortured with throes and longings, as of Hyde struggling after freedom.” The metaphor of addiction is unmistakable — Hyde is a craving that intensifies with every indulgence.

The Failure of the Experiment

Jekyll’s experiment fails for a specific reason: he cannot create a potion that separates the good side. The transformation only works one way — it releases evil but cannot isolate virtue. Jekyll explains: “Had I approached my discovery in a more noble spirit… all must have been otherwise.” He acknowledges that his motives were selfish from the start — he wanted freedom from moral responsibility, not genuine self-improvement. The novella argues that you cannot escape moral accountability by splitting yourself in two.

Jekyll’s final transformation is permanent because the original salt that powered the potion was impure — he cannot replicate it. He runs out of the crucial ingredient and knows that the next transformation will be his last. His statement ends with the knowledge that “this is the last time… that Henry Jekyll can think his own thoughts.” When Utterson breaks down the door, he finds Hyde dead by poison. Jekyll and Hyde die together because they are, and always were, one person.

The suicide is significant: Hyde chooses death rather than face justice. Even Hyde’s final act is selfish — he kills himself to avoid consequences, not out of remorse. Jekyll’s tragedy is that he created something he could not control and could not undo. The novella ends not with moral redemption but with destruction — a warning, not a comfort.

Key Fact

Hyde is smaller than Jekyll because “the evil side of my nature was less robust and less developed than the good.” Jekyll has spent years exercising virtue, so evil is stunted. But once released, Hyde grows stronger: the novella argues that evil is not a fixed quantity but a force that expands with indulgence. Repression does not destroy evil — it only stores it.

title: Context: Victorian Duality
content_html:
The Victorian World of Jekyll and Hyde

Robert Louis Stevenson published The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde in 1886, during the height of the Victorian era. The novella was an immediate sensation — 40,000 copies sold in the first six months. It struck a nerve because it exposed something Victorians desperately wanted to hide: the idea that respectable, civilised people harboured dark and violent desires beneath the surface.

Victorian society placed enormous value on respectability. A gentleman was expected to be rational, moral, restrained, and publicly virtuous. Yet behind the polished facades of London’s townhouses, many wealthy men led secret double lives — visiting opium dens, engaging in illicit relationships, and indulging desires they publicly condemned. Stevenson’s novella tore away this mask of respectability and forced his readers to confront their own hypocrisy.

Key Fact

Victorian gentlemen were expected to suppress all immoral urges. Jekyll creates Hyde not because he is unusually evil, but because the pressure to appear respectable is unbearable. Stevenson suggests that all humans have a dual nature — the Victorians simply refused to admit it.

Repression and the Double Life

The theme of repression runs through every page of the novella. Jekyll confesses in his final statement that he “learned to recognise the thorough and primitive duality of man.” He understood that every person contains both good and evil impulses. The problem was not the impulses themselves, but Victorian society’s insistence that they did not exist.

Jekyll’s transformation is not about gaining new evil qualities — it is about releasing desires he already possessed. He admits: “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde.” This early confidence reveals his fatal flaw: the belief that he can control the darkness within. Stevenson uses Jekyll’s gradual loss of control to warn that repression is not a solution — it only makes the eventual release of those desires more violent and destructive.

Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, just twenty-seven years before Stevenson’s novella. Darwin’s theory of evolution argued that humans had evolved from more primitive creatures. This horrified many Victorians because it suggested that beneath the veneer of civilisation, humans were still animals — capable of savage, instinctive violence. Hyde is repeatedly described in animalistic terms: he has “ape-like fury,” he is compared to a “troglodyte,” and witnesses describe something inhuman about his appearance. Stevenson draws on evolutionary anxiety to suggest that Hyde represents the primitive, pre-civilised self that lurks within every person.

The science versus religion debate was at its height. Many Victorians feared that if Darwin was right and humans were merely evolved animals, then morality itself had no divine foundation. Jekyll’s experiment — using science to separate good from evil — reflects this anxiety. His failure suggests that good and evil cannot be neatly divided, and that attempting to do so through science leads to catastrophe.

The Gothic Genre

Stevenson’s novella belongs to the Gothic tradition. Gothic literature explored the dark side of human nature, featuring supernatural events, psychological terror, and settings that reflected inner turmoil. Earlier Gothic novels like Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (1818) and Bram Stoker’s Dracula (1897) shared similar concerns about science overreaching its boundaries and the beast within civilised humanity.

Victorian Gothic moved the horror from remote castles into the heart of London. Stevenson’s fog-choked streets, sinister doorways, and respectable houses hiding terrible secrets reflect the idea that evil is not somewhere far away — it lives next door. The novella’s famous description, “The fog still slept on the wing above the drowned city,” turns London itself into a Gothic landscape where nothing is quite what it seems.

Key Fact

Victorian Gothic fiction brought horror into everyday urban settings. Stevenson uses London’s fog, gas-lit streets, and locked doors to create a world where respectability and monstrosity exist side by side. The Gothic setting mirrors the novella’s central theme: that darkness hides within the familiar.

Urban London and Social Division

The London of Jekyll and Hyde is a city of sharp contrasts. Wealthy areas like Cavendish Square sit close to dangerous, poverty-stricken slums like Soho. Jekyll’s grand house has a front entrance on a respectable street and a back entrance through a sinister, blistered door in a dingy lane. This physical layout mirrors the novella’s central metaphor: the respectable exterior and the hidden, shameful interior.

Stevenson grew up in Edinburgh, a city famously divided between the respectable New Town and the crime-ridden Old Town. He was the son of a devoutly religious lighthouse engineer but rebelled against his upbringing, exploring Edinburgh’s seedy underworld as a young man. He was also influenced by the real case of Deacon Brodie — an eighteenth-century Edinburgh cabinet-maker who was a respected citizen by day and a burglar by night. Brodie was eventually caught and hanged. Stevenson had a cabinet made by Brodie in his childhood bedroom, and later wrote a play about him. The duality of Jekyll and Hyde has its roots in Stevenson’s own city and personal experience.

The Edexcel Exam: What You Need to Know

For Edexcel 1ET0 Component 2, Section A, you will answer a two-part question on Jekyll and Hyde. Part (a) asks you to analyse an extract of around 400 words, focusing on language and how Stevenson creates meaning (AO1 + AO2). Part (b) asks you to explore a theme, character, or idea across the whole novella (AO1 + AO2). This is a closed book exam, so you must memorise key quotations. Context is not separately assessed, but strong responses weave contextual understanding into their analysis naturally.

title: Chapters 5-8: The Unravelling
content_html:
Chapter 5: Incident of the Letter

After the Carew murder, Utterson visits Jekyll in his “cabinet” above the laboratory. Jekyll is “deadly sick”, but insists he is “done with” Hyde. He produces a letter signed by Hyde absolving him of blame. Utterson’s clerk, Mr Guest, compares the handwriting to Jekyll’s own and declares it a forgery — the letter Jekyll wrote as Hyde matches Jekyll’s hand in every feature except the slope. Stevenson plants foreshadowing: the handwriting is literally the same because the writer is.

Key Fact

The forged letter is Stevenson’s cleverest hint. It lets the reader register suspicion without fully understanding the truth — training us to accept the later revelation as earned, not imposed.

Chapter 6: Remarkable Incident of Doctor Lanyon

Jekyll withdraws from society, then emerges briefly as his old self. Suddenly he refuses to see Utterson again. Utterson visits Lanyon instead and finds him transformed: “a death warrant written legibly upon his face… he had his death-warrant written there.” Lanyon says he has suffered “a shock” and refuses to name its cause. He dies within weeks, leaving a sealed letter marked “not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr Henry Jekyll.”

Stevenson uses Lanyon as a foil to Jekyll. Both are men of science, but Lanyon is “hide-bound”, sticking to “the practical side of medicine”. He cannot survive the knowledge Jekyll has gained. The contrast argues that some boundaries exist for good reason.

The 1880s were a decade of rapid scientific advance and anxiety: Darwin’s ideas were reshaping biology, and newer ideas about psychology (including those of William James and early Freud) were questioning the unity of the self. Stevenson’s Jekyll stands for the transgressive scientist who goes too far. Lanyon is the cautious alternative — and neither survives untouched.

The fear is not science itself, but the dissolution of the boundary between respectable professional and hidden appetites. This is why Stevenson makes the story about a doctor: the figure most trusted by Victorian society becomes the figure most dangerous.

Chapter 7: Incident at the Window

Utterson and Enfield again walk by the cursed court. Jekyll appears at the upper window, “infinite sadness” on his face. Utterson invites him down; Jekyll declines. Then “the smile was struck out of his face and succeeded by an expression of such abject terror and despair, as froze the very blood of the two gentlemen below… the window was instantly thrust down.” Stevenson compresses the whole tragedy into a single moment of horror and silence.

The chapter is short and placed centrally in the novella for good reason. Jekyll’s transformation must have started. Utterson and Enfield leave in silence, not daring to speak. Stevenson uses this silence to signal the limits of respectable language: there is nothing Victorian gentlemen can say about what they have just seen.

Chapter 8: The Last Night

Poole, Jekyll’s butler, arrives at Utterson’s in “white and shaky” terror. For a week a stranger has been locked in the cabinet crying out for a chemical that cannot be found. Poole is convinced the voice is not Jekyll’s: “That thing was not my master.” Utterson hears a voice whining: “For God’s sake have mercy!”

Utterson and Poole break down the door with an axe. They find Hyde’s body on the floor, a phial in his hand. There is no sign of Jekyll, but two documents: Jekyll’s will (rewritten to leave everything to Utterson), and a sealed packet — the “Full Statement” that forms Chapter 10. Stevenson leaves the chapter on a cliffhanger: the reader, like Utterson, does not yet know why Jekyll’s body is Hyde’s.

Key Fact

Poole notices three pieces of evidence: the voice sounds wrong, the hand glimpsed on the stair is ‘dwarfish’ and ‘hairy’, and a servant girl saw a creature ‘crying out like a rat’. The details rhyme with earlier descriptions of Hyde.

Jekyll’s cabinet sits above the dissecting theatre of an old surgeon. Stevenson deliberately layers the house: a respectable front, a working laboratory, an inner cabinet locked away. The architectural metaphor mirrors the Freudian-sounding model of the mind that the novella anticipates — surface, thought and hidden appetite.

Why These Chapters Matter

Chapters 5–8 are the unravelling. Stevenson switches from planting clues to accumulating them until the reader can no longer resist the conclusion. The forged letter, Lanyon’s death, Jekyll’s face at the window and Hyde’s body on the cabinet floor are arranged as a ladder down from respectable surface to exposed depth.

title: Context: Victorian Duality
content_html:
The Victorian Obsession with Respectability

Robert Louis Stevenson published The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde in 1886, at the height of the Victorian era. Victorian society was obsessed with respectability: gentlemen were expected to be rational, self-controlled, and morally upright in public. But beneath this polished surface, Victorian London harboured a hidden world of vice — prostitution, opium dens, gambling, and poverty. Stevenson’s novella explores this gap between public respectability and private desire.

The concept of duality was central to Victorian thought. Scientists, philosophers, and theologians all debated whether human nature was fundamentally good or evil. Stevenson dramatises this debate through Jekyll’s experiment: what if you could physically separate the two sides of your nature? The answer, the novella argues, is catastrophe — because good and evil are not separate entities but inseparable parts of the same person.

Key Fact

Victorian gentlemen maintained strict public respectability while often indulging private vices. Stevenson uses Jekyll’s experiment to expose this hypocrisy: Jekyll does not create evil — he releases the evil that was already inside him. Hyde is not a separate person but the part of Jekyll that society forced him to suppress. The novella argues that repression, not human nature, is the true danger.

Science and Religion

The 1880s were a period of intense conflict between science and religion. Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859) had challenged the biblical creation story and suggested that humans were descended from apes — an idea that horrified many Victorians. Hyde’s frequent description in animalistic terms (“like a monkey,” “snarled,” “ape-like fury”) connects him to Darwin’s theory: Hyde represents the primitive, animal nature that evolution revealed beneath the civilised surface.

Victorian readers feared degeneration — the idea that civilisation could go backwards, with humans reverting to a primitive state. Hyde embodies this fear: he is smaller than Jekyll (suggesting a less evolved form), described as “troglodytic” (cave-dweller), and provokes an instinctive revulsion in everyone who sees him. Characters struggle to describe what is wrong with Hyde: Enfield says he gave “a strong feeling of deformity,” though he cannot identify any specific feature. This indefinable wrongness suggests Hyde represents something beyond physical appearance — he is the degenerate self that Victorian society desperately wanted to deny.

Jekyll’s experiment can be read as a metaphor for the danger of scientific progress without moral restraint. He uses chemistry to achieve what nature would not allow: the separation of good and evil. But the experiment goes wrong because the separation is unnatural. Stevenson warns that science, like any form of power, requires ethical boundaries.

London as a Dual City

Stevenson sets the novella in London, a city that perfectly embodies Victorian duality. The respectable streets of the West End existed alongside the poverty and crime of the East End. Jekyll’s house has two faces: a handsome front door on a respectable street and a sinister back entrance (the “door” of Chapter 1) on a rundown lane. This architectural duality mirrors Jekyll’s psychological duality — the public face and the private shame are literally two sides of the same building.

Stevenson grew up in Edinburgh, a city with a literal split personality: the respectable New Town above and the cramped, vice-ridden Old Town below. He also knew about the real-life case of Deacon Brodie, an 18th-century Edinburgh cabinetmaker who was a respectable citizen by day and a burglar by night.
