These biographical connections help explain why duality fascinated Stevenson: he lived in a world where the gap between public and private selves was not just a literary idea but a daily reality.

Stevenson reportedly dreamed the central scene of the novella (the transformation) and wrote the first draft in three days. His wife Fanny criticised it for being too much of an adventure story, so he burned the manuscript and rewrote it as the psychological allegory we know today.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s house has a respectable front entrance and a sinister back door — two faces of the same building, just as Jekyll and Hyde are two faces of the same person. This architectural symbolism runs throughout the novella: Victorian London itself has a public face of respectability and a hidden world of vice.

title: Themes: Duality, Repression and Science
content_html:
Theme 1: Duality

Duality is the novella’s central theme. Stevenson argues that every human being contains both good and evil, and that trying to separate them is both impossible and dangerous.

Jekyll’s experiment is an attempt to split his “dual nature” into two separate beings. He describes “those provinces of good and ill which divide and compound man’s dual nature.” But the experiment fails because good and evil are not separable — they are woven into the fabric of every person.

Key Fact

Duality operates at every level of the novella: character (Jekyll/Hyde), setting (respectable front/decayed laboratory), narrative (multiple perspectives), and even the title (“Strange Case” suggests something that defies rational explanation).

Jekyll’s house has a grand, respectable front entrance on a “square of ancient, handsome houses” and a neglected back door opening onto a “blind forehead of discoloured wall.” The two entrances represent Jekyll’s two identities. Hyde uses the back door — literally entering through the hidden, shameful side of Jekyll’s life.

London itself is presented as a city of contrasts: wealthy streets sit alongside impoverished Soho; fog obscures the boundaries between respectability and vice. Stevenson uses the motif of fog to suggest that moral clarity is impossible in a society built on concealment.

Theme 2: Repression

Repression drives the entire plot. Jekyll creates Hyde because Victorian society demands that he suppress every “undignified” impulse. Rather than allowing himself small, harmless pleasures, he must maintain a facade of total respectability.

Stevenson’s message is clear: repression does not eliminate desire — it intensifies it. Jekyll’s suppressed urges, when finally released as Hyde, take their most extreme and violent form. If Jekyll had been able to live a more balanced life, he would never have needed the experiment.

Repression is not unique to Jekyll. Utterson denies himself the theatre and good wine. Enfield makes a “bargain” never to speak of Hyde again. Even Poole suppresses his fear until breaking point. Every character in the novella practises some form of self-denial, reflecting a society where concealment is a way of life.

Key Fact

The novella is set in an almost entirely male world. There are no significant female characters. This intensifies the theme of repression — Victorian masculinity demanded emotional restraint, self-control and the suppression of vulnerability.

Theme 3: Science and Its Limits

Jekyll’s experiment is a scientific endeavour — he mixes chemicals to create the transformative potion. But the experiment crosses a moral boundary. Lanyon calls it “unscientific balderdash,” not because the chemistry is wrong, but because it violates the natural order.

Stevenson wrote during a period of intense scientific debate. Darwin’s theory of evolution had shaken religious certainties. New research into psychology was suggesting that the human mind was more complex — and darker — than previously believed. The novella asks: should science explore every corner of human nature, even if the discoveries are horrifying?

Like Victor Frankenstein in Mary Shelley’s novel, Jekyll is a scientist who oversteps moral boundaries and creates a monster he cannot control. Both texts belong to the Gothic tradition, which frequently uses science as a source of horror. The message in both texts is similar: scientific ambition without moral restraint leads to destruction.

How the Themes Connect

The three themes are deeply interlinked. Victorian repression creates the conditions for Jekyll’s experiment. His scientific ambition provides the means. And the result reveals the duality at the heart of human nature. Stevenson’s novella is ultimately a warning: a society that refuses to acknowledge the darker side of human nature will be destroyed by it.

title: Chapters 1-4: Mystery & Terror
content_html:
Chapter 1: The Door and Enfield’s Story

The novella opens with two respectable gentlemen, Mr Utterson (a lawyer) and his kinsman Mr Enfield, walking through London. They pass a sinister door on a rundown street, and Enfield tells a strange story: he once witnessed a man “calmly trampl[e] over a child’s body” at a street corner. The man was Hyde. The crowd surrounded him, and Hyde paid compensation through a cheque signed by the respectable Dr Jekyll. Enfield’s reaction to Hyde is visceral: “I had taken a loathing to my gentleman at first sight.”

Stevenson uses mystery as his primary structural device. The reader, like Utterson, is given pieces of a puzzle without the full picture. We know Hyde is connected to Jekyll but not how. We know the door leads to Jekyll’s laboratory but not why Hyde uses it. The first four chapters build a web of second-hand narration: Enfield tells Utterson, Utterson investigates, but nobody speaks to Jekyll directly. This narrative structure mirrors the Victorian culture of secrecy — gentlemen do not ask uncomfortable questions.

Key Fact

Hyde tramples a young girl “calmly” — without remorse or hesitation. The word “calmly” is crucial: it shows that Hyde’s violence is not passionate rage but cold indifference to human suffering. He treats the child as though she does not exist. This establishes Hyde as a figure without empathy or conscience — the purely selfish part of human nature unleashed.

Chapter 2: Utterson’s Investigation

Utterson reads Jekyll’s will and discovers that everything is left to Hyde — including the provision that if Jekyll “disappears for any period exceeding three calendar months,” Hyde inherits. This alarming clause suggests either blackmail or something worse. Utterson visits Dr Lanyon, Jekyll’s old friend, who dismisses Jekyll’s recent scientific work as “unscientific balderdash.” The disagreement between the two doctors hints that Jekyll has crossed a moral boundary that Lanyon refuses to follow.

Utterson stakes out the sinister door and finally meets Hyde. His reaction is the same indefinable revulsion that every character experiences: “Mr Hyde was pale and dwarfish, he gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation.” Hyde produces a “disgusting” impression that Utterson cannot explain: “God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic.” The word troglodytic links Hyde to prehistoric humanity, reinforcing the degeneration theme.

Notice that characters consistently cannot describe what is wrong with Hyde. This is Stevenson’s deliberate technique: by making Hyde’s evil indefinable, he makes it universal. Hyde does not look like a specific type of villain — he embodies a feeling of wrongness that everyone recognises but nobody can articulate. In the exam, this is a powerful AO2 point about Stevenson’s language choices.

Chapter 3: Jekyll’s Reassurance

Utterson confronts Jekyll, who dismisses his concerns: “I can be rid of Mr Hyde… whenever I choose.” This is deeply ironic because the reader later learns that Jekyll is already losing control. Jekyll’s confidence is the confidence of an addict who believes he can stop at any time. Stevenson uses proleptic irony throughout: statements that seem reassuring on first reading become ominous once the truth is revealed.

Chapter 4: The Carew Murder

Hyde’s violence escalates dramatically. He murders Sir Danvers Carew, a respected MP, in a frenzied attack witnessed by a maidservant: “Mr Hyde broke out of all bounds and clubbed him to the earth. And next moment, with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim underfoot and hailing down a storm of blows, under which the bones were audibly shattering.” The language is extraordinarily violent: “ape-like fury,” “trampling,” “bones audibly shattering.” Stevenson moves from the cold trampling of a child to a savage murder, showing Hyde’s escalating loss of control.

Carew is described as “an aged beautiful gentleman with white hair” who approaches Hyde “with a very pretty manner of politeness.” The contrast between Carew’s gentleness and Hyde’s savagery is absolute. Carew represents everything that Victorian respectability values: age, beauty, courtesy, and public service. Hyde’s destruction of him symbolises the assault of the primitive, selfish self on civilised values.

The maidservant who witnesses the murder does so by moonlight — she is at an upstairs window, looking down. This vertical perspective (observer above, crime below) mirrors the structure of Jekyll’s house and Victorian society itself: respectability lives upstairs, while violence happens in the streets below.

Key Fact

The Carew murder is described with escalating violence: “with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim underfoot and hailing down a storm of blows, under which the bones were audibly shattering.” “Ape-like” links to degeneration, “trampling” echoes the child incident (showing escalation), and “bones audibly shattering” uses sound imagery to make the violence disturbingly real.

title: Language, Structure and Narrative Perspective
content_html:
Language: Key Techniques

Stevenson’s language is precise and purposeful. Every word choice contributes to the novella’s atmosphere of mystery, horror and moral unease.

Hyde is consistently described using animalistic imagery. He moves with “ape-like fury,” is called “troglodytic” (cave-dwelling), and hisses “like a cornered snake.” This language links Hyde to degeneration theory — the Victorian fear that humans could reverse-evolve into primitive creatures. By making Hyde animal-like, Stevenson suggests that evil is not a moral failing but a biological reality lurking inside everyone.

Characters repeatedly struggle to describe Hyde. Enfield says he is “not easy to describe” and gives “a strong feeling of deformity.” Utterson notes “deformity without any nameable malformation.” This technique of describing something by saying it cannot be described is called apophasis. It makes Hyde more terrifying because the reader must imagine the horror for themselves.

This linguistic vagueness also reflects Victorian society’s inability to confront evil directly. The characters can sense that Hyde is wrong, but their respectable vocabulary has no words for what they are feeling.

Key Fact

Stevenson uses pathetic fallacy extensively. London’s fog, darkness and gaslight mirror the moral confusion and hidden evil at the heart of the story. The city itself becomes a character — concealing, distorting and threatening.

Structure: Three Narratives

The novella’s structure is one of its most distinctive features. It uses three different structural layers:

Chapters 1–8: Third-person narrative focused on Utterson. The reader shares his limited perspective, piecing together clues alongside him.

Chapter 9: Lanyon’s first-person letter. A shift to direct testimony from someone who witnessed the transformation.

Chapter 10: Jekyll’s first-person “full statement.” The final revelation, told by the man at the centre of the mystery.

Each narrative layer reveals more of the truth. Utterson sees the outside; Lanyon witnesses the transformation; Jekyll explains everything. This structure mirrors the peeling away of a disguise — the deeper we go, the closer we get to the horrifying reality beneath the respectable surface.

The use of epistolary elements (letters and written statements) is also significant. The truth can only be told in writing, after death. In Victorian society, some truths were literally unspeakable — they could only be committed to paper and sealed away.

Key Fact

The novella ends with Jekyll’s statement, not with Utterson’s reaction. The reader never learns what happens after Jekyll’s death. This open ending forces the reader to draw their own conclusions about the meaning of the story.

Narrative Perspective and Reliability

Stevenson carefully controls what the reader knows and when. Utterson is a reliable narrator in the sense that he reports honestly what he sees. But his perspective is limited — he cannot understand what is happening because it is beyond rational explanation.

Jekyll, by contrast, is an unreliable narrator. Even in his “full statement,” he distances himself from Hyde (“He, I say — I cannot say I”) and minimises his own responsibility. The reader must decide how much to trust Jekyll’s version of events.

Stevenson draws on several Gothic conventions:

The doppelgänger — Hyde is Jekyll’s dark double, a common Gothic motif representing the hidden self.

The mad scientist — Jekyll, like Frankenstein, conducts an experiment that creates a monster beyond his control.

The discovered manuscript — The truth is revealed through found documents (Lanyon’s letter, Jekyll’s statement), a technique used by Gothic writers to create a sense of authenticity.

Atmosphere of dread — Fog, darkness, locked doors and screaming winds create a persistent sense of menace.

title: Context: Victorian Duality
content_html:
Stevenson and Victorian Duality

Robert Louis Stevenson published The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde in 1886, during a period of intense anxiety about the duality of human nature. Victorian society demanded absolute respectability from its professional classes. Doctors, lawyers, and gentlemen were expected to be morally upright in every aspect of their lives. But beneath this polished surface, London harboured a dark underworld of vice, crime, and moral transgression.

Stevenson understood this hypocrisy firsthand. He grew up in respectable Edinburgh society but was drawn to the city’s seedy Old Town. His novella asks a question that terrified Victorians: what if every respectable man contains a hidden self, capable of terrible things? Dr Jekyll is the answer — a “large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty” who conceals desires he cannot reconcile with his public reputation.

Key Fact

Victorian society demanded absolute respectability from professional men. Stevenson uses Jekyll’s dual identity to expose the hypocrisy of this demand: the more rigidly society enforces moral perfection, the more violently the repressed self erupts. Hyde is not a separate person — he is Jekyll’s hidden desires given physical form.

The Gothic Tradition

Stevenson writes within the Gothic tradition, which uses horror and the supernatural to explore psychological and social fears. Gothic fiction features doubles, secrets, transgression, and the return of the repressed. Jekyll and Hyde combines all of these: Jekyll is both protagonist and antagonist; the secret of his double life drives the plot; his experiments transgress the boundaries of science and morality.

The novella also draws on the doppelgänger tradition — the idea that every person has a shadow-self. Hyde is Jekyll’s doppelgänger: smaller, younger, and purely evil because he represents only the repressed desires that Jekyll has spent his life concealing. Stevenson takes the Gothic convention and gives it a scientific framework: Jekyll does not summon a demon but creates Hyde through chemistry.

Stevenson was fascinated by the real-life case of Deacon Brodie, an eighteenth-century Edinburgh cabinet-maker who was a respected citizen by day and a burglar by night. Brodie was eventually caught and hanged. Stevenson kept a cabinet made by Brodie in his bedroom as a child, and the story haunted him. Brodie proved that the respectable surface could conceal a criminal interior — the central idea of Jekyll and Hyde.

Victorian Science and Morality

The 1880s were a period of rapid scientific advancement that unsettled religious certainties. Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859) had suggested that humans evolved from animals, raising the terrifying possibility that our ‘civilised’ behaviour was merely a thin veneer over animal instincts. Stevenson taps directly into this anxiety: Hyde is described in animalistic terms — “like a monkey,” with “ape-like fury” — suggesting he represents the primitive creature beneath the civilised gentleman.

Jekyll’s experiment also raises questions about the ethics of transgressive science. He attempts to separate the good and evil in human nature through chemistry — an act of hubris that echoes Frankenstein. Like Shelley’s Victor, Jekyll discovers that the attempt to transcend natural limits leads to destruction. The potion does not purify Jekyll; it unleashes his worst impulses without restraint.

Key Fact

Hyde is repeatedly described in animalistic and evolutionary terms: ‘like a monkey,’ ‘ape-like fury,’ ‘hardly human.’ This connects to post-Darwinian anxiety that civilisation is a thin veneer. Jekyll’s experiment is transgressive science: attempting to separate good from evil, he instead unleashes the primitive self.

The Novella’s Structure

Stevenson structures the novella as a mystery. We see Hyde through multiple perspectives before we understand his connection to Jekyll. Utterson the lawyer investigates; Enfield witnesses Hyde’s violence; Lanyon sees the transformation and dies from shock. The truth is withheld until the final two chapters: Lanyon’s narrative and Jekyll’s full statement. This structure mirrors the theme of concealment: just as Jekyll hides Hyde from society, Stevenson hides the truth from the reader.

The multiple narrators also mean that no single perspective is complete. Utterson sees only surfaces. Lanyon sees the scientific horror. Jekyll’s statement provides the interior truth. Stevenson suggests that identity is never fully knowable — we only ever see partial views of other people, and even of ourselves.

Stevenson’s London is both realistic and symbolic. The fog, darkness, and labyrinthine streets create a Gothic atmosphere, but they also represent the moral confusion of a city where respectable facades conceal hidden vices. Jekyll’s house has two faces: the respectable front on the square and the sinister back door on the by-street through which Hyde enters and exits. The house is Jekyll’s duality made architectural.

title: Character Analysis
content_html:
Dr Henry Jekyll

Jekyll is a wealthy, respected doctor who appears to be a model Victorian gentleman. He is “a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty, with something of a slyish cast perhaps, but every mark of capacity and kindness.” The word “slyish” is crucial — even in this positive description, Stevenson hints at something hidden. Jekyll’s tragedy is not that he is evil but that he is human: he contains both good and evil and cannot accept this duality. His experiment is an attempt to be respectable and indulge his desires — to have it both ways without moral consequences.

Jekyll is ultimately a tragic figure. His flaw is not vice but the desire to escape moral accountability. He wants to sin without guilt, to be Hyde without being Hyde’s consequences. His confession reveals genuine self-knowledge (“I was in no sense a hypocrite”) but also self-deception (“I can be rid of Mr Hyde whenever I choose”). The gap between his self-knowledge and his self-deception is what destroys him.

Key Fact

Jekyll has genuine self-knowledge (“both sides of me were in dead earnest”) but also dangerous self-deception (“I can be rid of Mr Hyde whenever I choose”). He understands his duality intellectually but cannot control it practically. This makes him a tragic figure: he sees the truth but cannot act on it. His experiment is an attempt to cheat morality, and it destroys him.

Mr Edward Hyde

Hyde is described through other characters’ reactions because Stevenson never gives a detailed physical description. He is “pale and dwarfish,” gives an “impression of deformity without any nameable malformation,” and provokes instant revulsion. His violence escalates from cold indifference (trampling the child) to savage fury (the Carew murder). Hyde represents the id — the selfish, instinctive part of human nature freed from conscience.

Utterson is described as “ausere with himself” — he suppresses his own pleasures (he drinks gin to mortify his taste for wine, and has not visited a theatre for twenty years). He represents the ideal Victorian gentleman: loyal, discreet, and restrained. But his very discretion is part of the problem. He suspects something is wrong with Jekyll for months but does not ask the right questions because Victorian propriety forbids intrusion into another gentleman’s private affairs.

Utterson also functions as the reader’s proxy: we discover information as he does. His rational, legal mind makes him a reliable narrator, but his Victorian restraint means he cannot see what is right in front of him. Stevenson uses Utterson to show how respectability itself becomes an obstacle to truth.

Lanyon dismissed Jekyll’s work as “unscientific balderdash” before the events of the novella. He represents conventional Victorian science — empirical, cautious, and unwilling to explore dangerous territory. When he witnesses the transformation, the shock kills him. Lanyon is Stevenson’s comment on the limits of the conventional Victorian worldview: it can function only as long as certain truths remain hidden. Once exposed, it shatters.

Lanyon and Jekyll are foils: Jekyll pushes beyond accepted boundaries while Lanyon stays safely within them. Both are destroyed — Jekyll by his recklessness and Lanyon by the truth he refused to consider. Stevenson suggests there is no safe position: ignoring human duality is as dangerous as confronting it.

Key Fact

Each character represents a different response to duality: Jekyll (attempts to separate good and evil), Hyde (evil without conscience), Utterson (refuses to look too closely), Lanyon (destroyed by the truth he cannot accept). Together, they explore the Victorian dilemma: how do you live with the knowledge that civilised people contain primitive impulses?

title: Setting & Narrative
content_html:
London as a Character

Stevenson’s London is a city of contrasts. Respectable streets give way to “dingy” lanes without warning. Fog descends and lifts unpredictably, concealing and revealing. The fog is not just weather — it is a metaphor for the obscured truth that pervades the novella. When Utterson investigates, he moves through “a great chocolate-coloured pall lowered over heaven… the fog still slept on the wing of the morning.” The language of sleep and darkness suggests a city that does not want to see clearly.

Settings in the novella consistently reflect the theme of duality. Scenes of respectability are disrupted by violence: the Carew murder happens on a moonlit street, the trampling occurs at a busy corner. Stevenson shows that evil does not confine itself to dark alleys — it erupts in public spaces, breaking through the surface of civilised life.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s house is the novella’s most important setting. The handsome front door opens onto a respectable street; the sinister back door (where Hyde enters) opens onto a rundown lane. The two entrances represent Jekyll’s dual nature — the public face of respectability and the private entrance for vice. The laboratory connecting them is where the transformation occurs: the space where public and private selves meet.

Narrative Structure: Multiple Perspectives

Stevenson uses an unusual narrative structure. The first eight chapters are third-person narration focused through Utterson. Chapters 9 and 10 switch to first-person accounts from Lanyon and Jekyll respectively. This structure creates a layered revelation: the reader gets the “outside view” first (what people see) and the “inside view” last (what Jekyll feels). The truth is discovered in reverse — the explanation comes after the events, forcing the reader to re-evaluate everything they thought they knew.

The novella’s characters are almost entirely male. There are no significant female characters: the maidservant witnesses the Carew murder, and the child and the old woman are brief presences. This homosocial world reflects Victorian gentlemen’s culture of clubs, professional partnerships, and male friendships. It also intensifies the theme of secrecy: these men are bound by codes of discretion that prevent them from asking each other uncomfortable questions.

Some critics read the absence of women as significant for what it conceals. Jekyll’s “undignified pleasures” are never specified, and Victorian readers would have understood the implication: the vices of gentlemen were sexual, financial, or narcotic — but always hidden. Stevenson’s vagueness is deliberate: by not naming Jekyll’s sins, he makes them universal.

Gothic Techniques

Stevenson employs classic Gothic techniques: dark settings, locked doors, mysterious sounds, and a sense of building dread. But he adapts the Gothic for a modern urban setting. The terror of Jekyll and Hyde is not supernatural — it is psychological and scientific. The most frightening element is not a ghost or a monster but the discovery that the monster lives inside the respectable doctor next door.

Throughout the novella, characters use the language of concealment. Enfield tells Utterson: “I make it a rule of mine: the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask.” Utterson reflects: “If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek.” Even when characters resolve to investigate, they wrap their intentions in wordplay and deflection. Stevenson shows that Victorian language itself is a form of concealment — a way of talking about things without naming them.

This linguistic concealment mirrors the novella’s larger argument: Victorian society has developed sophisticated ways of hiding its dual nature. The polished language, the codes of propriety, the refusal to ask uncomfortable questions — these are not just social habits but defence mechanisms against the terrifying truth that civilised people contain savage impulses.

Key Fact

Stevenson’s narrative structure (outside view first, inside view last) forces the reader to discover the truth in reverse. His language of concealment (characters refusing to name what they see) mirrors Victorian society’s defence against uncomfortable truths. Both techniques make the reader experience the same discomfort as the characters: we know something is wrong but cannot quite name it.

title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
content_html:
Theme: Duality of Human Nature

The novella’s central theme is that every human being contains both good and evil. Jekyll articulates this directly: “Man is not truly one, but truly two.” His experiment attempts to separate these halves, but fails catastrophically because — as he also admits — “all human beings are commingled out of good and evil.” The two cannot be divided. Attempting to do so does not purify Jekyll; it creates a creature of pure evil (Hyde) while leaving Jekyll weaker and less able to resist.

Stevenson extends duality beyond Jekyll. Utterson has a “dualistic” character: austere yet tolerant. London itself is dual: respectable by day, sinister by night. Even the narrative structure has two faces: the mystery conceals the confession. Duality is not one character’s problem — it is the human condition, and Victorian society’s refusal to acknowledge it is what makes it destructive.

Key Fact

‘Man is not truly one, but truly two’ — but the two halves are ‘commingled’ (inseparable). Jekyll’s experiment fails because separating good from evil is impossible. The potion does not purify; it unleashes. Stevenson argues that acknowledging duality is healthier than repressing it.

Theme: Repression and Its Consequences

Victorian society demanded that professional men suppress all ‘unrespectable’ desires. Jekyll embodies this: “I concealed my pleasures; and when I reached years of reflection… I stood already committed to a profound duplicity of life.” The repression does not eliminate desire — it compresses it. When Hyde finally emerges, he does so with explosive, disproportionate violence. The trampled child, the murdered Carew — these acts are consequences of decades of suppressed impulse.

Stevenson’s message is clear: repression breeds monsters. A society that demands moral perfection will produce spectacular moral failure. The novella is both a psychological study of one man and a social critique of an entire culture.

Jekyll’s experiment raises questions about scientific ethics. He uses chemistry to alter human nature itself — an act of hubris that parallels Frankenstein and anticipates twentieth-century anxieties about genetic engineering. Lanyon, the conventional scientist, dismisses Jekyll’s work as ‘unscientific balderdash’ — but his death after witnessing the transformation suggests that conventional science cannot cope with unconventional truth. Stevenson presents science as both powerful and dangerous: capable of revealing hidden truths but also of unleashing hidden evils.

Theme: Secrecy and Surveillance

The novella is saturated with secrecy. Jekyll hides his dual life. Utterson investigates but respects privacy. Enfield and Utterson agree never to discuss what they’ve seen. Lanyon’s letter is sealed until Jekyll’s death. The narrative is a series of locked doors, sealed documents, and withheld information. Stevenson shows that Victorian respectability was maintained through collective agreement not to look too closely — a conspiracy of silence that enabled both individual and social hypocrisy.

Key Fact

Secrecy pervades every level: Jekyll hides Hyde, Utterson hides his suspicions, Enfield hides what he saw, the narrative hides its truth in sealed documents. Stevenson critiques a culture where respectability depends on collective silence.

Exam Preparation

Your 19th-century novel question may offer a choice between an extract-based task and a discursive task, both assessing AO1, AO2 and AO3. Extract-based: Analyse the passage closely (language, imagery, symbolism), then connect to the novella as a whole. Discursive: Build an argument responding to a statement with evidence from across the text. Both require integrated AO1+AO2+AO3 in every paragraph. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact format, mark weightings and timing.

Key exam strategies for Jekyll and Hyde: (1) Always treat settings as symbolic — the house, the fog, London’s geography. (2) Analyse Hyde’s physical descriptions as connecting to Darwinian/evolutionary anxiety. (3) Discuss the narrative structure as a method — multiple perspectives, sealed documents, delayed revelation. (4) Embed context: Victorian respectability, post-Darwin science, Gothic tradition.

Point: Stevenson uses Hyde’s physical appearance to embody post-Darwinian anxiety. Evidence: Hyde moves with ‘ape-like fury’ and is described as ‘like a monkey.’ Analysis: The simian imagery connects Hyde to evolutionary regression — the fear that beneath civilised behaviour lies a primitive animal self. The word ‘fury’ suggests this self is not just present but violent, explosive when released. Context: Darwin’s theory that humans evolved from primates terrified Victorians who believed in human exceptionalism. Stevenson weaponises this fear through Hyde’s body.

title: Chapters 9-10: The Revelations
content_html:
Chapter 9: Dr Lanyon’s Narrative

The novella’s final two chapters abandon Utterson’s perspective entirely. Chapter 9 is Lanyon’s sealed letter, opened after his death. It reveals what destroyed him. Jekyll had written to Lanyon with urgent, desperate instructions: go to Jekyll’s cabinet, collect a specific drawer of chemicals, and bring it to Lanyon’s house. At midnight, a visitor would come to collect them.

The visitor who arrives is Hyde — small, dressed in clothes far too large for him (Jekyll’s clothes), shaking with desperate need. Hyde mixes the chemicals into a potion and offers Lanyon a choice: leave the room, or stay and witness something that will “stagger the unbelief of Satan.” Lanyon, driven by scientific curiosity, chooses to stay.

Key Fact

Hyde drinks the potion and transforms into Jekyll before Lanyon’s eyes. Lanyon describes his reaction: “like a man restored from death.” But this is not a resurrection — it is the opposite. Seeing the transformation destroys Lanyon’s entire worldview. Everything he believed about science, about the separation of mind and body, about the nature of reality, is shattered in a single moment. He never recovers. Stevenson implies that some truths are too terrible for the human mind to survive.

The phrase “like a man restored from death” is richly ambiguous. On the surface, it describes Jekyll’s reappearance. But it also suggests that Jekyll is not truly alive — he has been living a kind of death since creating Hyde. The simile hints at resurrection, but Stevenson subverts the religious connotation: this is not a divine miracle but a scientific abomination.

Chapters 1–8 are narrated from Utterson’s perspective — a measured, rational, legal viewpoint. Chapter 9 shifts to Lanyon’s voice: still rational but now fractured by horror. This structural shift is deliberate. Utterson’s calm, investigative narration cannot contain the truth. Stevenson needs a different voice — someone who has witnessed the transformation firsthand. Lanyon’s narrative is a testimony from a man who has seen the impossible. His clinical language (“I saw what I saw, I heard what I heard”) struggles to process the experience, and this struggle makes the horror more convincing.

Chapter 10: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case

The final chapter is Jekyll’s own confession, written as he feels the last transformation approaching — the one from which he will never return. It reveals everything. Jekyll explains that from a young age, he was aware of a profound duality in his nature. He felt torn between his desire for pleasure and his need to maintain the respectable public image demanded by Victorian society.

Jekyll writes: “Man is not truly one, but truly two.” This is the novella’s central statement. Jekyll discovered, through his experiments, that the human personality is not a single, unified self but a battleground between opposing forces. He believed that if he could separate these forces — extract the evil and contain it in a separate body — both halves could live freely. The good Jekyll could be virtuous without the weight of dark desires; the evil Hyde could indulge without guilt.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s experiment fails for a devastating reason: evil is stronger than good. Hyde is pure evil, but Jekyll is not pure good — he remains a mixture. Over time, Hyde grows stronger while Jekyll weakens. Jekyll confesses: “I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self.” The balance tips irreversibly. The transformations begin happening involuntarily, without the potion, and Jekyll can no longer control when Hyde emerges.

The Loss of Control

Jekyll describes the terrifying moment he woke up one morning and realised he had transformed into Hyde in his sleep. He looked down at his hand and saw it was “lean, corded, knuckly” — Hyde’s hand, not his own. The synecdoche of the hand is powerful: hands represent agency, identity, and moral choice. Jekyll’s hand becoming Hyde’s hand means he has lost control over his own body and moral identity.

From this point, Jekyll needs the potion not to become Hyde but to become himself again. The default state has shifted. He is trapped: running out of the original chemical compound, unable to reproduce it because a crucial impurity in the original batch cannot be replicated. Jekyll writes with increasing desperation, knowing that the next transformation will be permanent.

Stevenson offers a psychological explanation for Hyde’s increasing dominance. Each time Jekyll becomes Hyde, he indulges desires that were previously repressed. Rather than satisfying these desires, the indulgence strengthens them. Hyde is smaller than Jekyll at first because the evil side has been suppressed for years. But as Hyde is given more freedom, he grows — both in physical stature and in power over Jekyll’s consciousness. Stevenson’s message is clear: evil does not diminish when it is fed. Repressed desires, once released, do not return quietly to their cage.

Jekyll’s confession also reveals that he enjoyed being Hyde. He describes the “leap of welcome” he felt with each transformation — the exhilaration of freedom from social constraint. This enjoyment makes Jekyll complicit in Hyde’s crimes. He is not an innocent victim of his experiment; he is an addict who cannot stop returning to the drug.

The Final Transformation

Jekyll’s statement ends mid-sentence. He writes: “I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end.” The reader understands that as Jekyll writes these final words, Hyde is taking over for the last time. There is no dramatic death scene for Jekyll — he simply ceases to exist, consumed by the creature he created. Hyde, trapped in the cabinet and facing arrest for Carew’s murder, takes cyanide rather than face justice.

Stevenson denies the reader a conventional resolution. Jekyll does not defeat Hyde. Good does not triumph over evil. The novella ends with destruction: Jekyll gone, Hyde dead, Lanyon dead, and the truth contained in documents that the reader has been allowed to witness but the wider world of the story has not. The secrets of Victorian gentlemen die with them.

title: Character Analysis
content_html:
Dr Henry Jekyll

Jekyll is a wealthy, respected London doctor — “a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty.” He is the embodiment of the Victorian gentleman: educated, charitable, sociable, and admired by his peers. But Jekyll is also deeply conflicted. He confesses in Chapter 10 that he was born with a strong sense of duality: an urge towards pleasure that clashed with his need for public respectability. Rather than accept this tension as part of being human, Jekyll tries to eliminate it through science.

Jekyll’s tragic flaw is not that he is evil, but that he refuses to accept the duality of his own nature. He believes he can separate good from evil cleanly — “if each could be housed in separate identities, life would be relieved of all that was unbearable.” This is both scientifically arrogant and psychologically naive. Stevenson shows that attempting to deny or divide the self leads to destruction, not liberation.

Key Fact

Jekyll is complicit in Hyde’s crimes. He describes a “leap of welcome” each time he transforms, and admits that Hyde’s pleasures were “undignified” but that he enjoyed them. Jekyll’s tragedy is that he is an addict: he knows the experiment is destroying him but cannot stop. His confession — “I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self” — reveals that Jekyll understands his own destruction but is powerless to prevent it.

Mr Edward Hyde

Hyde is Jekyll’s alter ego — the physical embodiment of everything Jekyll has repressed. He is small, pale, and “dwarfish,” because the evil side of Jekyll’s nature has been suppressed for years and is therefore underdeveloped. Every person who encounters Hyde feels instinctive revulsion, yet nobody can explain exactly what is wrong with him: he gives “an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation.”

Hyde’s violence escalates throughout the novella. He tramples a child with casual cruelty, then murders Sir Danvers Carew with “ape-like fury.” The animalistic language connects Hyde to atavism — the Darwinian fear that humans could regress to a pre-civilised state. Hyde is not a monster from outside; he is the monster within, the primitive self that Victorian respectability tried to deny.

Hyde is not a separate person but a part of Jekyll. This is why Hyde is smaller — he is a fraction of Jekyll’s complete personality, not a whole individual. As the novella progresses, Hyde grows larger and more powerful because the evil side is being exercised and strengthened. Stevenson presents Hyde as a shadow self — the part of a person they refuse to acknowledge. The horror of the novella is not that Hyde exists, but that he exists within all of us. Jekyll says “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde,” but this proves impossible precisely because Hyde is not separate from Jekyll — he is Jekyll, unmasked.

Mr Gabriel John Utterson

Utterson is Jekyll’s lawyer and the novella’s central consciousness for the first eight chapters. He is described as “lean, long, dusty, dreary,” a man who suppresses his own pleasures (he enjoys wine and theatre but denies himself both). He is the model of Victorian self-restraint: loyal, discreet, non-judgemental, and determined to protect his friends’ reputations above all else.

Utterson’s role is structural as well as thematic. He is the reader’s surrogate, piecing together clues about the Jekyll–Hyde mystery. His declaration — “If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek” — sets up the detective narrative. But Utterson is also limited by his own respectability. He assumes the worst explanation is blackmail; the truth (that Jekyll and Hyde are the same person) is literally unthinkable to a rational Victorian mind. Stevenson uses Utterson to show that loyalty and discretion, while admirable, can also prevent people from confronting dangerous truths.

Dr Hastie Lanyon

Lanyon is a conventional, respected doctor and one of Jekyll’s oldest friends. He represents mainstream Victorian science: cautious, empirical, and deeply sceptical of anything unorthodox. He had dismissed Jekyll’s research as “unscientific balderdash” long before the events of the novella. When Lanyon witnesses Hyde’s transformation into Jekyll in Chapter 9, the experience destroys him. He describes Jekyll as appearing “like a man restored from death,” but it is Lanyon himself who is effectively killed by the revelation.

Key Fact

Lanyon serves as a foil to Jekyll. Where Jekyll pushes beyond the boundaries of accepted science, Lanyon stays firmly within them. Their professional disagreement reflects the Victorian tension between progress and caution, between exploring dangerous knowledge and respecting limits. Lanyon’s death after witnessing the transformation implies that those limits exist for a reason.

Richard Enfield and Poole

Enfield is Utterson’s cousin — a “well-known man about town” who witnesses Hyde’s trampling of the girl in Chapter 1. His description of Hyde as bearing “Satan’s signature upon a face” is one of the novella’s most vivid phrases. Enfield represents the ordinary observer: shocked by evil but ultimately choosing not to investigate further. He and Utterson agree not to discuss the matter again — a very Victorian response to scandal.

Poole, Jekyll’s butler, is a working-class character in a novella dominated by upper-class professionals. His role in Chapter 8 is crucial: he is the one who recognises that the voice behind the locked door is not his master’s. “Have I been twenty years in this man’s house, to be deceived about his voice?” Poole’s instinct and emotional intelligence prove more reliable than Utterson’s legal reasoning. He weeps openly, breaks social conventions by demanding Utterson’s help, and provides the axe to break down the door. Stevenson uses Poole to suggest that emotional honesty and practical action are more effective than the educated gentleman’s tendency to deliberate and defer.

The novella is almost entirely populated by men. Women appear only as victims (the trampled girl) or peripheral witnesses (the maidservant). This all-male world reflects the homosocial nature of Victorian professional life, where reputation was maintained through male networks of loyalty and discretion. The absence of women intensifies the claustrophobic atmosphere of secrecy and repression that defines the novella.

title: Chapters 4–6: The Carew Murder and Incident at the Window
content_html:
Chapter 4: The Carew Murder Case

Nearly a year after the events of Chapter 2, Hyde commits a far more serious crime. A maid witnesses him brutally beating an elderly gentleman — Sir Danvers Carew, a respected MP — to death with a heavy walking stick. The attack is unprovoked: Carew had simply asked Hyde for directions.

The violence is extreme. The maid describes how Hyde “broke out in a great flame of anger” and “clubbed him to the earth” with “ape-like fury.” The cane snaps in half under the force of the blows. Stevenson uses this scene to show that Hyde’s evil is escalating — from trampling a child to committing murder.

Key Fact

The broken walking stick belonged to Utterson — he had given it to Jekyll as a gift years earlier. This detail physically connects Jekyll to the murder and foreshadows the eventual revelation that they are the same person.

Utterson takes the police to Hyde’s rooms in Soho. The setting is significant: Soho was one of Victorian London’s most disreputable areas, associated with poverty, crime and vice. Hyde’s rooms are furnished with luxury items but show signs of a hasty departure — ashes in the fireplace, a burnt cheque book. Hyde has vanished.

Stevenson describes Soho in fog and darkness: “a district of some city in a nightmare.” The symbolism is clear — Soho represents the hidden, immoral side of London that respectable Victorians preferred to ignore. The fog that blankets the streets mirrors the moral confusion surrounding Jekyll’s double life.

Chapter 5: The Letter

Utterson visits Jekyll, who is visibly shaken. Jekyll claims he has received a letter from Hyde promising to disappear forever. Jekyll asks Utterson to judge whether the letter should be given to the police. Utterson agrees to keep it.

Later, Utterson’s clerk Mr Guest notices that the handwriting in Hyde’s letter is remarkably similar to Jekyll’s own handwriting — just slanted differently. Utterson is horrified: “Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer!” He assumes Jekyll is covering for Hyde, not yet suspecting the truth.

Key Fact

The matching handwriting is a crucial clue that Jekyll and Hyde are the same person. Stevenson plants this evidence for the reader, but Utterson — bound by Victorian propriety — refuses to follow it to its logical conclusion.

Chapter 6: Remarkable Incident of Dr Lanyon

Time passes. Hyde has disappeared, and Jekyll seems renewed — sociable, charitable and “at peace.” For two months, he appears to have conquered his demons. But then Jekyll suddenly withdraws from society, refusing all visitors.

When Utterson visits Dr Lanyon, he finds him shockingly changed — pale, thin and visibly dying. Lanyon says he has received “a shock” from which he will never recover. He refuses to discuss Jekyll, saying only: “I wish to see or hear no more of Dr Jekyll … I am quite done with that person.”

Lanyon’s transformation is one of the novella’s most powerful moments. A once-confident, robust man has been reduced to a dying shell. Stevenson withholds the cause of his horror — we only learn what Lanyon witnessed in Chapter 9. This delayed revelation builds suspense and suggests that the truth is so terrible it literally kills the man who sees it.

Lanyon dies shortly afterwards. He leaves Utterson a sealed letter, only to be opened after Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson — ever the man of principle — respects Lanyon’s wishes and does not open it.

Stevenson uses sealed letters as a structural device throughout the novella. Jekyll’s will, Lanyon’s letter and Jekyll’s own “full statement” are all documents that contain the truth but are withheld from the reader. This creates a pattern of secrets and revelations that mirrors the theme of hidden identity.

title: Characters: Jekyll and Hyde
content_html:
Dr Henry Jekyll

Jekyll is a wealthy, respected doctor and scientist. He is “a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty” who hosts dinner parties and donates to charity. He represents the ideal Victorian gentleman: moral, successful and generous.

But Jekyll harbours a secret. In his “full statement,” he confesses that he always felt a duality within himself. He describes “those provinces of good and ill which divide and compound man’s dual nature.” He was not a hypocrite in the usual sense — he genuinely wanted to be good. But the pressure of Victorian respectability meant he had to suppress his desires entirely, rather than finding a healthy balance.

Key Fact

Jekyll does not create Hyde to be evil. He creates Hyde to experience freedom — to indulge his “undignified” pleasures without risking his reputation. The tragedy is that separating good from evil makes both sides more extreme.

Jekyll’s story follows a classic tragic pattern. His hamartia (tragic flaw) is his belief that he can control the experiment. At first, he transforms voluntarily and enjoys the freedom. Then Hyde grows stronger. The transformations become involuntary. Finally, the potion stops working, and Jekyll is trapped as Hyde permanently. His suicide is the only escape.

Stevenson suggests that repression is the true cause of Jekyll’s downfall. If Victorian society had allowed Jekyll to express all sides of himself, he would never have needed the experiment.

Mr Edward Hyde

Hyde is Jekyll’s alter ego — the physical embodiment of everything Jekyll represses. He is described as small, pale, and giving an impression of deformity. Characters who encounter him feel instinctive disgust but cannot explain why.

Hyde’s appearance is deliberately vague. Stevenson uses words like “troglodytic,” “ape-like” and “hardly human” to suggest he is less evolved than a normal person. This connects to Victorian fears about degeneration — the idea that humanity could evolve backwards.

Key Fact

Hyde is smaller than Jekyll because, as Jekyll explains, his evil side had “less exercise” — it had been suppressed for years. This physical detail reinforces the idea that repression stunts part of the self rather than eliminating it.

Hyde’s violence escalates throughout the novella. He tramples a child (Chapter 1), murders Sir Danvers Carew with “ape-like fury” (Chapter 4), and becomes increasingly uncontrollable. Each act is more extreme than the last. Stevenson uses this escalation to show that evil, once released from restraint, does not stay moderate — it grows.

Crucially, Hyde feels no guilt. Jekyll describes him as “pure evil.” This distinguishes Hyde from Jekyll, who does feel remorse but uses the separation of identity to avoid taking full responsibility.

The Relationship Between Jekyll and Hyde

Jekyll and Hyde are not simply “good” and “evil.” Jekyll himself is not entirely good — he created Hyde out of selfish desire for freedom. And Hyde is not a separate person but a part of Jekyll that has always existed. The novella’s central argument is that everyone contains both good and evil, and that trying to deny this makes things worse.

Even in his final confession, Jekyll refers to Hyde in the third person: “He, I say — I cannot say I.” He tries to maintain the fiction that Hyde is a separate being. But this is self-deception. Jekyll created Hyde, enjoyed being Hyde, and is ultimately destroyed by Hyde. They are the same person.

Stevenson uses this self-deception to criticise Victorian society more broadly. Just as Jekyll refuses to acknowledge his darker self, Victorian society refused to acknowledge the poverty, vice and cruelty that existed beneath its respectable surface.

title: Chapters 5-8: The Unravelling
content_html:
Chapter 5: The Incident of the Letter

After the Carew murder, Utterson visits Jekyll. He finds Jekyll in his cabinet — the private room behind his laboratory — looking “deadly sick.” Jekyll claims he has received a letter from Hyde, promising never to return. Jekyll tells Utterson the relationship is over. But when Utterson’s clerk, Mr Guest, compares Hyde’s letter with a sample of Jekyll’s handwriting, he discovers the two are almost identical. Utterson is horrified: “Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer!” He suspects Jekyll is covering for Hyde, but the real explanation — that they are the same person — is far worse than anything Utterson can imagine.

Stevenson uses this chapter to tighten the mystery. The matching handwriting is a crucial clue, but Utterson’s rational mind cannot make the impossible leap to the truth. His reaction reveals the limits of Victorian rational thinking: some truths are too terrible for the logical mind to accept.

Chapter 6: Remarkable Incident of Dr Lanyon

Time passes. Hyde has vanished. Jekyll appears reformed — sociable, generous, and devout. For two months, he seems like his old self. Then, suddenly, Jekyll withdraws entirely. He refuses visitors. Utterson visits Dr Lanyon, hoping for information, and is shocked by what he finds.

Lanyon is a changed man. He looks as if he has received a death sentence: his face is pale, he has visibly aged, and his manner is one of deep, unshakeable terror. He declares that he has had a shock and will never recover: “I have had a shock, and I shall never recover. It is a question of weeks.” When Utterson mentions Jekyll, Lanyon reacts violently, refusing to hear his name. Something has happened between them that has destroyed Lanyon’s health and their friendship forever.

Key Fact

Lanyon dies shortly after this chapter. He leaves a sealed letter for Utterson, not to be opened until after Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Lanyon’s death is caused not by physical injury but by the psychological horror of what he has witnessed. Stevenson uses Lanyon’s fate to show that confronting the truth about human duality can be fatal — some knowledge destroys.

Lanyon and Jekyll represent opposing approaches to science. Lanyon is a conventional doctor — cautious, empirical, and grounded in accepted knowledge. Jekyll pushes beyond these boundaries, exploring what he calls “transcendental medicine.” Lanyon had earlier dismissed Jekyll’s work as “unscientific balderdash.” The irony is devastating: Lanyon’s rational worldview cannot survive contact with the truth. When he finally witnesses Hyde transform into Jekyll, the sight destroys him. Stevenson implies that Victorian rationalism is a fragile defence against the darker realities of human nature.

Chapter 7: Incident at the Window

This is the shortest chapter in the novella. Utterson and Enfield pass Jekyll’s window during another walk. They see Jekyll sitting by the open window, looking like a prisoner. He begins to talk to them, and for a moment it seems normal. Then “the smile was struck out of his face and succeeded by an expression of such abject terror and despair” that Utterson and Enfield can only walk away in silence, deeply shaken.

Stevenson never explains what happens in this moment. The reader later understands that Jekyll was beginning to transform involuntarily — Hyde was emerging without the potion. The horror is intensified because it happens in broad daylight, in a respectable setting, witnessed by two gentlemen who cannot comprehend what they have seen. Their reaction — walking away in appalled silence — is itself a comment on Victorian repression: faced with something terrible, they choose not to speak of it.

Chapter 8: The Last Night

Jekyll’s butler, Poole, arrives at Utterson’s house in a state of terror. He believes his master has been murdered and that Hyde is locked in the cabinet. For a week, a voice from behind the locked door has been crying out for a particular chemical, sending servants on frantic errands to pharmacists across London — but every sample is rejected as impure. Poole has heard the voice change: “Have I been twenty years in this man’s house, to be deceived about his voice?”

Poole and Utterson break down the door with an axe. Inside, they find Hyde’s body on the floor, still twitching, with a crushed phial of cyanide in his hand. He has killed himself. Jekyll is nowhere to be found. On the desk lie three documents: a new will naming Utterson as beneficiary, a short note, and a thick sealed packet containing Jekyll’s full confession.

Key Fact

The breaking down of the cabinet door is the novella’s climactic moment. Throughout the story, doors have symbolised the barrier between the respectable exterior and the hidden truth. When Utterson and Poole smash through, they are literally breaking through the wall of secrecy that has protected Jekyll’s double life. What they find — Hyde’s body, not Jekyll’s — is the final mystery, resolved only in the last two chapters.

Poole is a servant, not a gentleman, and his role in the climax is significant. He crosses social boundaries by going to Utterson’s house and insisting on action. His loyalty to Jekyll overrides Victorian class conventions. Poole’s terror is physical and visceral — he weeps, his face is white, and he can barely speak. Stevenson uses Poole’s raw emotion to contrast with Utterson’s controlled, rational approach. It is Poole, not Utterson, who drives the action: he provides the axe, he identifies the changed voice, and he forces the confrontation. The servant sees the truth more clearly than the lawyer.

The chapter is structured as a thriller. Stevenson builds suspense through the sound of footsteps pacing behind the locked door (“weeping like a woman or a lost soul”), the desperate search for the chemical, and the moment when Poole describes seeing the creature in the corridor — small, masked, and crying out. The reader’s heart races alongside Utterson’s. By the time the door is broken down, the tension is almost unbearable.

title: Chapters 1–3: The Door, the Will and Dr Jekyll
content_html:
Chapter 1: Story of the Door

The novella opens with Mr Utterson and his cousin Richard Enfield on their regular Sunday walk. They pass a mysterious, neglected door in an otherwise respectable street. Enfield tells Utterson a disturbing story: he once saw a small, ugly man trample over a young girl in the street “like some damned Juggernaut.”

The man was Mr Hyde. When confronted, Hyde showed no remorse but agreed to pay compensation. He disappeared through the mysterious door and returned with a cheque signed by Dr Jekyll. Enfield and Utterson agree never to speak of the matter again — a very Victorian response, prioritising discretion over truth.

Key Fact

The trampling of the girl is the reader’s first encounter with Hyde’s violence. Stevenson deliberately makes the victim a child to emphasise Hyde’s complete lack of moral boundaries.

Chapter 2: Search for Mr Hyde

Utterson goes home and reads Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde in the event of Jekyll’s death or “disappearance.” The word “disappearance” troubles Utterson deeply. He visits Dr Lanyon, an old friend of Jekyll’s, who dismisses Jekyll’s recent scientific work as “unscientific balderdash.”

Utterson begins to stake out the mysterious door. When he finally meets Hyde, he is struck by an overwhelming sense of repulsion. He describes Hyde as giving “an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation.” This is crucial — Hyde’s evil is felt rather than seen.

Throughout the novella, characters struggle to describe what is wrong with Hyde. Enfield says he is “not easy to describe” and gives “a strong feeling of deformity.” Utterson notes “deformity without any nameable malformation.” Stevenson deliberately makes Hyde’s appearance vague and unsettling. This mirrors the Victorian difficulty in confronting evil directly — they can sense it but cannot name it.

Chapter 3: Dr Jekyll Was Quite at Ease

Utterson visits Jekyll at one of his dinner parties. Jekyll is charming, sociable and entirely at ease — the complete opposite of Hyde. When Utterson raises concerns about the will, Jekyll becomes evasive and asks Utterson to drop the subject. He insists: “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde.”

This chapter establishes the contrast between Jekyll and Hyde. Jekyll is warm, generous and respected; Hyde is cold, violent and repulsive. Yet Jekyll is clearly hiding something — his discomfort when Utterson mentions Hyde reveals the anxiety beneath his polished surface.

Key Fact

Jekyll’s claim that he “can be rid of Mr Hyde” at any time proves tragically wrong. This is an example of dramatic irony — the reader later discovers that Jekyll loses control of the transformations entirely.

Stevenson uses Utterson as the main narrative perspective for most of the novella. As a lawyer, Utterson is rational, restrained and trustworthy — making him a reliable guide for the reader. But his rationality also limits what we can know. He cannot understand Jekyll’s experiment because it is beyond rational explanation. The restricted perspective builds suspense and mirrors Victorian society’s refusal to look too closely at uncomfortable truths.

Stevenson’s Methods in Chapters 1–3

These opening chapters establish several key techniques that Stevenson uses throughout the novella:

Mystery and withholding: Stevenson reveals information slowly. The reader, like Utterson, must piece together clues. The connection between Jekyll and Hyde is not explained until the final two chapters.

Setting as symbolism: The mysterious door — blistered, neglected, with “no bell nor knocker” — represents the hidden side of Jekyll’s life. It is the back entrance to his laboratory, a passage between his respectable home and his secret world.

Fog and darkness: London is repeatedly described in terms of fog, shadows and gaslight. The fog symbolises the obscured truth and moral confusion at the heart of the story.
